scenes.title: Computer Systems
scenes.body: Chapter 1 This chapter shows you how a computer thinks in 0s and 1s, how logic gates turn those bits into decisions, how software is planned and built step by step, and how data travels across a network. These three ideas — digital logic, software development and communication models — are the foundation of everything else in Computer Science.

scenes.title: 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities
scenes.body: Everything around you that can be measured or counted is a quantity . Quantities come in two kinds. Discrete quantities are separate, countable items with specific values. You can count them one by one: 1, 2, 3 … There is nothing "in between". You cannot have 2.5 students in a classroom. Continuous quantities can take any value within a range. They flow smoothly without breaks. Water can be 30 °C, 30.5 °C, 30.51 °C, and so on — there is always another value in between. Stairs have fixed steps (discrete).

scenes.title: 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities · 2
scenes.body: A ramp lets you stand at any point (continuous). Stairs vs Ramp. On stairs you can only stand on step 1, 2 or 3 — that is discrete data. On a ramp you can stand at any height — that is continuous data. Ask yourself: "Do I count it or measure it?" Count → discrete. Measure → continuous. Students sometimes say "money is continuous because amounts are large". No — rupees and paisa are counted in fixed units, so money is discrete. Size does not matter; what matters is whether values in between are possible. 1.

scenes.title: 1.1.2 Introduction to Digital Systems
scenes.body: A digital system is an electronic system that uses only two values: 0 and 1 . These two values are called binary digits , or bits for short. 0 represents OFF, LOW, or FALSE. 1 represents ON, HIGH, or TRUE. Why only two values? Because it is easy for an electronic circuit to tell "voltage present" from "no voltage". Every number, letter, photo and song in a computer is finally stored as a long pattern of these bits. Advantages of digital systems Examples of digital systems Computers: process data as 0s and 1s.
scenes.urdu: ڈیجیٹل نظام صرف دو قیمتیں استعمال کرتا ہے: 0 اور 1، جنہیں بِٹ (Bit) کہتے ہیں۔ 0 کا مطلب بند، کم یا غلط ہے اور 1 کا مطلب چالو، زیادہ یا درست ہے۔ ڈیجیٹل نظام قابلِ بھروسا، درست، بنانے میں آسان اور سافٹ ویئر سے قابو میں رہنے والے ہوتے ہیں۔

scenes.title: 1.1.2 Introduction to Digital Systems · 2
scenes.body: Smartphones: store photos and music as binary data. Digital cameras: capture images as binary code. Why is copying digital data "accurate"? Step 1: A song is stored as bits, for example 10110010… Step 2: When you copy it to a USB, the computer copies each bit exactly: 1 stays 1, 0 stays 0. Step 3: Even after 100 copies the bits are identical, so the song sounds the same. An old cassette tape (analog) loses a little quality every time it is copied. Think of a bit as a light switch: it is either ON (1) or OFF (0).

scenes.title: 1.1.3 Analog and Digital Signals
scenes.body: A signal is a changing voltage (or other quantity) that carries information. Analog signals are continuous signals that change smoothly over time, like a sine wave . Examples: the human voice, a traditional mercury thermometer. Digital signals have only two levels: HIGH (1) and LOW (0) . They jump instantly between these values, which creates a square wave . Example: computer data. An analog signal changes smoothly; a digital signal jumps between only two levels. Why is digital more resistant to noise?

Step 3: The receiver only asks "Is it closer to HIGH or LOW?" 4.6 V is still read as 1 and 0.3 V is still read as 0. The data is perfect. Step 4: In an analog signal, every exact value carries meaning, so 4.6 V instead of 5 V really changes the sound or reading. The noise cannot be removed. Analog = A smooth curve. Digital = Doorsteps.

scenes.title: 1.1.4 Boolean Algebra
scenes.body: Boolean algebra was developed by the English mathematician George Boole . It is a kind of algebra that deals with only two values: TRUE (1) and FALSE (0) . It is the foundation of digital electronics and computer programming — every if condition in a program is a small piece of Boolean algebra. Some simple rules (laws) follow directly from the meaning of AND, OR and NOT. They are useful when you check or simplify answers: Using a law: Simplify Y = A'B + AB.

scenes.title: 1.1.5 Boolean Operations
scenes.body: There are three basic Boolean operations. Every other operation can be made from them. 1. AND operation ( · ) — gives output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1 . Expression: Y = A · B (often written just AB). 2. OR operation ( + ) — gives output 1 when ANY input is 1 . Expression: Y = A + B . 3. NOT operation ( ' or ¯ ) — inverts (flips) the input. If the input is 1 the output is 0, and if the input is 0 the output is 1. It is a unary operation, meaning it works on only one operand.
scenes.urdu: AND آپریشن تب ہی 1 دیتا ہے جب تمام ان پٹ 1 ہوں (دو تالوں والا دروازہ)۔ OR آپریشن تب 1 دیتا ہے جب کوئی ایک ان پٹ بھی 1 ہو (دو دروازوں والا کمرہ)۔ NOT آپریشن ان پٹ کو الٹ دیتا ہے اور صرف ایک ان پٹ پر کام کرتا ہے، اس لیے اسے یونری (Unary) کہتے ہیں۔

scenes.title: 1.1.6 Truth Tables
scenes.body: A truth table shows all possible input combinations and the output for each one, for a logic gate or a circuit. It is the "complete record" of how the circuit behaves. How to create a truth table: Count the number of inputs ( n ). Calculate total rows = 2 n . List all input combinations in binary counting order (0, 1, 2, 3 … in binary). Calculate the output for each combination.

scenes.title: 1.1.7 Logic Gates (Basic Gates: AND, OR, NOT)
scenes.body: Logic gates are electronic circuits that perform Boolean operations. They take one or more input bits and produce one output bit. They are the building blocks of all digital systems — a processor contains billions of them. The three basic gates match the three basic operations: the AND gate , the OR gate and the NOT gate (also called an inverter ). Symbols of the basic gates. AND has a flat back and round front ("D" shape); OR has a curved back and pointed front; NOT is a triangle with a small circle (bubble).
scenes.urdu: لاجک گیٹس الیکٹرانک سرکٹ ہیں جو بولین آپریشن انجام دیتے ہیں اور تمام ڈیجیٹل نظاموں کی بنیادی اینٹیں ہیں۔ AND گیٹ صرف تب 1 دیتا ہے جب دونوں ان پٹ 1 ہوں، OR گیٹ صرف تب 0 دیتا ہے جب دونوں ان پٹ 0 ہوں، اور NOT گیٹ ان پٹ کو الٹ دیتا ہے۔

scenes.body: AND gate — Y = A · B OR gate — Y = A + B NOT gate — Y = A' A school bell circuit. The bell (Y) should ring when the timer says "period over" (A = 1) and the school is open (B = 1). Step 1: The bell needs both conditions, so use an AND gate: Y = A · B. Step 2: Sunday, timer fires: A = 1, B = 0 → Y = 1 · 0 = 0. No bell. Step 3: Monday, timer fires: A = 1, B = 1 → Y = 1. The bell rings. If instead the bell should ring when either the timer fires or the principal presses a button, you would use an OR gate.

scenes.title: 1.1.7 Universal Logic Gates (NAND and NOR)
scenes.body: NAND means "NOT AND": it is an AND gate followed by a NOT. NOR means "NOT OR": an OR gate followed by a NOT. On the symbol, the NOT is shown as a small bubble at the output. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any logic circuit in the world can be built using only NAND gates (or only NOR gates) . Factories like this: they can mass-produce one type of chip and build everything from it. NAND = AND symbol + bubble. NOR = OR symbol + bubble.
scenes.urdu: NAND کا مطلب ہے NOT AND اور NOR کا مطلب ہے NOT OR۔ انہیں یونیورسل (عالمگیر) گیٹ کہتے ہیں کیونکہ صرف NAND یا صرف NOR گیٹس سے دنیا کا کوئی بھی لاجک سرکٹ بنایا جا سکتا ہے۔ NAND صرف تب 0 دیتا ہے جب دونوں ان پٹ 1 ہوں، اور NOR صرف تب 1 دیتا ہے جب دونوں ان پٹ 0 ہوں۔

scenes.title: 1.1.7 Universal Logic Gates (NAND and NOR) · 2
scenes.body: NAND (NOT AND) — Y = (A · B)' NOR (NOT OR) — Y = (A + B)' Show that a NAND gate can work as a NOT gate. Step 1: Connect the same input A to both inputs of the NAND gate. Then Y = (A · A)'. Step 2: Since A · A = A, we get Y = A'. Step 3: Check: A = 0 → (0·0)' = 0' = 1. A = 1 → (1·1)' = 1' = 0. This is exactly the NOT truth table. In the same way, a NOR gate with both inputs tied together gives (A + A)' = A'. And a NAND followed by a NAND-as-NOT gives ((A·B)')' = A·B, an AND gate. This is why they are "universal".
scenes.speak: NAND (NOT AND) , Y (A B)' NOR (NOT OR) , Y (A + B)' Show that a NAND gate can work as a NOT gate. Step 1: Connect the same input A to both inputs of the NAND gate. Then Y (A A)'. Step 2: Since A A A, we get Y A'. Step 3: Check: A 0 to (0 0)' 0' 1. A 1 to (1 1)' 1' 0. This is exactly the NOT truth table. In the same way, a NOR gate with both inputs tied together gives (A + A)' A'. And a NAND followed by a NAND-as-NOT gives ((A B)')' A B, an AND gate. This is why they are "universal".

scenes.title: 1.1.7 Advanced Logic Gates (XOR and XNOR)
scenes.body: XOR (Exclusive OR) gives output 1 when the inputs are different . Expression: Y = A ⊕ B . In terms of basic operations, A ⊕ B = A'B + AB'. XNOR (Exclusive NOR) is XOR followed by NOT. It gives output 1 when the inputs are the same . Expression: Y = (A ⊕ B)' = A'B' + AB. The XOR symbol is an OR symbol with an extra curved line at the input side. XNOR adds a bubble at the output. XOR = OR symbol with an extra curve at the back. XNOR = XOR symbol + bubble.

scenes.title: 1.1.8 – 1.1.10 Logic Expressions, Minterms and Maxterms
scenes.body: A logic expression (Boolean expression) combines variables with operations, for example Y = A + B'·C. To evaluate it correctly you must follow the order of precedence , just like BODMAS in maths: 1. Parentheses ( ) → 2. NOT ( ' ) → 3. AND ( · ) → 4. OR ( + ) Worked example 1: truth table of Y = A + B' · C Step 1: 3 inputs, so 8 rows. Step 2: Precedence: first find B' (NOT), then B'·C (AND), then A + (B'·C) (OR). Make a column for each step. Step 3: Y = 1 in rows 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 (decimal).
scenes.urdu: ایکسپریشن حل کرتے وقت ترتیب یہ ہے: پہلے قوسین، پھر NOT، پھر AND اور آخر میں OR۔ منٹرم (Minterm) اُن قطاروں سے بنتا ہے جن کا آؤٹ پٹ 1 ہو؛ اس میں 0 والے متغیر پر بار (A') لگتی ہے۔ میکس ٹرم (Maxterm) اُن قطاروں سے بنتا ہے جن کا آؤٹ پٹ 0 ہو؛ اس میں 1 والے متغیر پر بار لگتی ہے۔

scenes.body: A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 0, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 1. OR-ing all the minterms gives the SOP expression. Maxterm (used in POS — Product of Sums): a sum (OR) of all the variables, written for a row whose output is 0 . A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 1, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 0. AND-ing all the maxterms gives the POS expression. Final SOP expression: Y = A'B + AB. Final POS expression: Y = (A + B)(A' + B). Both describe the same table.

scenes.title: 1.1.11 Logic Diagrams
scenes.body: A logic diagram shows how logic gates are connected to create a circuit. It is a "picture" of a Boolean expression. To draw one, use the order of precedence: the operation with the highest priority is drawn first (nearest the inputs), and the last operation is the gate that gives the final output. Example 1: Draw the logic diagram for Y = A · B + C. Step 1: Find the operations: AND ( · ) and OR ( + ). Step 2: AND has higher precedence than OR, so draw the AND gate first, with inputs A and B. Its output is A · B.

scenes.title: 1.1.13 Karnaugh Maps (K-Maps)
scenes.body: A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical tool used to simplify Boolean expressions . It is a grid of cells — one cell for each row of the truth table. The cells are arranged so that neighbouring (adjacent) cells differ by only ONE bit . This ordering is called Gray code . You write the output (1 or 0) of each row into its cell, then group the 1s in rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 (powers of 2). Each group becomes one simple term. This simplifies the equation without long algebra.

scenes.title: 1.1.13 Karnaugh Maps (K-Maps) · 2
scenes.body: Two-variable K-map (A, B) 2 variables need 2 2 = 4 cells. Three-variable K-map (A, B, C) 3 variables need 2 3 = 8 cells. The columns follow the Gray code sequence 00, 01, 11, 10 (not 00, 01, 10, 11). This makes adjacent cells differ by only one variable. Grouping rules Group only 1s. Groups must be rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 — never 3, 5 or 6. Make groups as large as possible . Bigger groups give simpler terms. Use as few groups as possible , but every 1 must be in at least one group.

scenes.title: 1.1.13 Karnaugh Maps (K-Maps) · 3
scenes.body: Overlapping is allowed — a 1 may be used in more than one group. Wrapping around the edges is allowed : a cell in the far-left column is adjacent to the cell in the far-right column (BC = 00 is next to BC = 10). To read a group: variables that change (0 to 1) inside the group are eliminated . Variables that stay the same are kept — plain if they stay 1, complemented if they stay 0.

scenes.title: LogiSim Evolution: Simulation Tool
scenes.body: LogiSim Evolution is a free graphical tool for designing and simulating logic circuits . "Simulating" means the computer pretends to be the real circuit: you can switch inputs on and off and watch the output change. It lets you see the truth tables and Boolean expressions you learn in theory. 1. The interface areas The main areas of the LogiSim Evolution window. Wiring colours during simulation Colours like a traffic light: Green means "working" (bright = 1, dark = 0).

scenes.title: Building a Circuit in LogiSim
scenes.body: Step by step: building Y = A · B Select the AND gate from the Toolbar (or from the Gates library) and place it on the canvas. Select the Input Pin (square icon with a 0) and place two pins to the left of the gate. Label them A and B. Select the Output Pin (circle icon with a 0) and place it to the right. Label it Y. Use the Wiring Tool to click and drag wires from the input pins to the AND gate's input ports. Wires must be horizontal or vertical. Wire the gate's output to the output pin Y.

scenes.title: 1.2.1 – 1.2.3 Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
scenes.body: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process that guides software development from beginning to end. It ensures clear goals, better planning, risk reduction and high quality . Without it, teams forget features, go over budget and deliver buggy software. SDLC has 6 phases : 1. Requirement Analysis → 2. System Design → 3. Implementation → 4. Testing → 5. Deployment → 6.

scenes.title: 1.2.4 The Waterfall Model
scenes.body: The Waterfall model is a linear, sequential approach to the SDLC. Each phase must be completed before the next one begins, like water falling down steps. There is no easy way to go back to a previous phase. The Waterfall model: each phase "falls" into the next, in one direction only. When to use it Requirements are clear, fixed and well understood. The project is small to medium in size. The technology is stable (not new or experimental). Case study: Al-Noor Library Management System.

The project is small to medium in size. The technology is stable (not new or experimental). Case study: Al-Noor Library Management System.

scenes.title: 1.2.4 The Waterfall Model · 2
scenes.body: The textbook uses this system as a Waterfall case study because the requirements were 100% fixed before coding began . Step 1: The librarian listed exactly what was needed: add books, issue books, return books, calculate fines. Nothing would change. Step 2: Because the list was fixed, the team could finish the full design, then all the coding, then all the testing, in order. Step 3: Every phase produced a document, so the library has a complete record for future maintenance. Waterfall = water only flows downwards.

scenes.title: 1.2.4 The Agile Model
scenes.body: The Agile model is an iterative approach: the software is built in small, repeated cycles called sprints (usually 2–4 weeks long). Each sprint plans, builds and tests a small part of the software, and then shows it to the customer. Customer feedback is gathered continuously and used in the next sprint. Plan → Design → Build → Test → Review & feedback → Next sprint ↺ When to use it Requirements are unclear or may change. The customer wants frequent progress updates (early delivery).

scenes.body: Both models follow the same SDLC phases. scenes.title: 1.3.1 – 1.3.4 Communication Models and the OSI 7-Layer Model
scenes.body: A communication model explains how data travels from one device to another through a network. Because sending data is complicated, the job is split into layers ; each layer does one part of the job and passes the data to the next layer. The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model was developed by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) in 1984 . It divides communication into 7 layers .

scenes.title: 1.3.5 – 1.3.6 TCP/IP Model vs OSI Model
scenes.body: The OSI model is mainly a reference model used for teaching and design. The TCP/IP model is the practical model used on the real Internet . It condenses the 7 OSI layers into just 4 layers . How the 7 OSI layers map onto the 4 TCP/IP layers. Where does each protocol/device go in TCP/IP? HTTP (OSI layer 7) → TCP/IP Application . SSL/TLS (OSI layer 6) → TCP/IP Application (layers 7, 6, 5 are merged). UDP (OSI layer 4) → TCP/IP Transport . IP and routers (OSI layer 3) → TCP/IP Internet .

scenes.title: Computational Thinking & Algorithm
scenes.body: Chapter 2 This chapter teaches you how to think like a computer scientist: break a problem into parts, spot patterns, ignore what does not matter, and write clear step-by-step algorithms. You will then learn four famous algorithms — Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Linear Search and Binary Search — and how to judge and choose between them.

You will then learn four famous algorithms , Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Linear Search and Binary Search , and how to judge and choose between them.

scenes.title: 2.1 Computational Thinking
scenes.body: Computational Thinking (CT) is a systematic approach to solving problems. "Systematic" means you follow a fixed, organised method instead of guessing. CT involves four activities: Decomposition — breaking a big problem down into smaller parts. Pattern recognition — identifying things that repeat or follow a rule. Abstraction — hiding (ignoring) details that do not matter. Algorithms — developing clear step-by-step instructions to solve the problem. CT is not "thinking like a computer".

scenes.title: 2.2 Algorithm
scenes.body: An algorithm is a step-by-step logical procedure used to solve a problem. It is conceptual in nature (it is an idea, a plan) and completely independent of any programming language . The same algorithm can be written later in Python, C++ or Java. A good algorithm has: Input — the data it starts with. Clear steps — each step has only one meaning. A definite end — it must finish after a limited number of steps. Output — the result it produces.

The same problem written both ways: print whether a number is even or odd.

scenes.title: 2.3.1 Decomposition
scenes.body: 2.3 Algorithmic Strategies for Problem Solving. An algorithmic strategy is a general method that helps you design an algorithm. The three strategies in your syllabus are decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction. Decomposition is a problem-solving technique in which a complex task or system is broken down into smaller, manageable parts. By dividing a big problem into simpler steps, it becomes easier to understand, develop and solve. Each small part is called a sub-task (or sub-problem).

scenes.title: 2.3.2 Pattern Recognition
scenes.body: Pattern recognition is the process of identifying regularities, repetitions or rules in data. It helps in reducing the overall complexity of an algorithm and forms the foundation of concepts such as loops . How it works — ask yourself three questions: What is repeating? What changes in a predictable way? Can I generalise this (write one rule that works for every case)? Example: Triangle of stars Step 1 — What repeats? Every row prints stars. Step 2 — What changes predictably?

scenes.title: 2.3.3 Abstraction
scenes.body: Abstraction means hiding unnecessary features and focusing only on the essential ones needed to solve a problem. It reduces complexity by ignoring what is not important (the noise ). When you apply abstraction you sort details into three groups: Necessary steps — the core logic that never changes. Changes based on the situation — these become variables (inputs) in the algorithm. Abstraction items (noise) — details you can ignore completely.

scenes.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort
scenes.body: Bubble Sort is an elementary sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly comparing adjacent (side-by-side) elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. In each pass, the largest remaining value "bubbles up" to the end of the list, like an air bubble rising to the top of water. So after pass 1 the largest value is in the last place, after pass 2 the second largest is in second-last place, and so on. A list of N items needs N − 1 passes , and pass K makes N − K comparisons .

scenes.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Selection Sort
scenes.body: Selection Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly selecting the smallest element from the unsorted portion of the list and moving it to its correct position at the front. Think of it as filling seats from the front: first find who belongs in position 1, then position 2, and so on. In the textbook version, the element at position K is compared with every element after it; whenever a smaller one is found, the two are swapped. So at the end of pass K, the K-th smallest value sits in position K.

scenes.title: 2.4.2 Searching Algorithms: Binary Search
scenes.body: Binary Search is a highly efficient search algorithm that works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Crucial limitation: it only works on a SORTED list. Three variables mark the part of the list still being searched: BEG (low) — first position of the current part. END (high) — last position of the current part. MID = INT((BEG + END) / 2) — the middle position. INT means "drop the decimal part". At each step compare the item with DATA[MID]: Equal → found, stop.

scenes.title: 2.5 Evaluation Criteria of Algorithm
scenes.body: Many algorithms can solve the same problem. To judge which is better, we evaluate them on three criteria: correctness , efficiency and clarity . 2.5.1 Correctness An algorithm is correct if: its output matches the expected outcomes; it handles edge cases gracefully (unusual inputs such as an empty list, 0, a negative number, or an item that is not present); it is guaranteed to finish — no infinite loops.
scenes.urdu: کسی الگورتھم کو تین معیارات پر پرکھا جاتا ہے: درستگی (Correctness) یعنی درست نتیجہ دے، غیر معمولی صورتوں کو سنبھالے اور ہمیشہ ختم ہو؛ کارکردگی (Efficiency) یعنی کم وقت اور کم میموری استعمال کرے؛ اور وضاحت (Clarity) یعنی پڑھنے، سمجھنے اور تبدیل کرنے میں آسان ہو۔ درستگی جانچنے…

scenes.title: 2.5 Evaluation Criteria of Algorithm · 2
scenes.body: We test correctness with a trace table (dry run): we feed sample inputs and record every value by hand, then compare the result with what we expect. Trace table example: Even/Odd checker. Rule: divide the number by 2; if the remainder is 0 it is Even, otherwise Odd. All three results match what we expect, so the algorithm is correct for these inputs. The same check in Python: A good tester would also try the edge case 0 (remainder 0 → Even, which is correct).

scenes.title: 2.5 Evaluation Criteria of Algorithm · 3
scenes.body: 2.5.2 Efficiency We measure algorithm efficiency through time (speed) and space (memory). The key question is: how fast does it run as the input size grows — does it scale well? Computer scientists describe growth with Big O notation . It counts roughly how many steps are needed for N items: O(1) — constant: same time, whatever N is. O(log N) — logarithmic: grows very slowly (Binary Search). O(N) — linear: double N, double the time (Linear Search).

scenes.title: 2.6 How to Decide Which Algorithm to Use
scenes.body: Before choosing an algorithm, ask three questions: What is the input size? (10 items or 10 million?) Is the data sorted? Do we need speed or memory efficiency? Simple decision guide: If searching on unsorted data → use Linear Search . If searching on sorted data → use Binary Search . If data needs ordering → use a sorting algorithm. What is the task? → Need order? → Sorting algorithm → Need to find? Is data sorted?

scenes.title: 3.1 Programming
scenes.body: Computers are "dumb" machines. They are very fast, but they cannot think or do anything on their own. They need exact, step-by-step instructions . A set of instructions given to a computer is called a program . The language used to write these instructions is called a programming language . Writing programs is called programming , and the person who writes them is a programmer . Think of a recipe. A cook follows the recipe line by line: "boil water, add rice, wait 15 minutes".

The three levels of programming languages, with a sample line from each. Common high-level languages Same task, three levels. Suppose you want to copy a value. Machine language: a pattern like 01010101 — you would need a chart to know what it means. Assembly: MOV AX, BX — "move the value in register BX into register AX".

scenes.title: 3.3 Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
scenes.body: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is a software tool that helps programmers write, run and manage code in one place . It is a complete workspace for programming. "Integrated" means many tools are joined together in one window. Key features of an IDE: Code Editor: where you write and edit code. Syntax Highlighting: colours different parts of the code (keywords, strings, numbers) to make it easier to read. Auto-completion: suggests code while you type (type pri and it offers print ).

scenes.title: 3.4 Fundamentals of Python Programming
scenes.body: The basic structure of a Python program is simple and clear. A program takes data, processes it using statements , and finally shows output . Python runs the statements top to bottom, one after another (sequentially). A statement is one complete instruction, usually written on one line, such as print("Hi") or x = 5 . 1. Comments ( # ) — Comments are notes written in the code for humans . They start with the # symbol. The Python interpreter completely ignores them. Use them to explain what your code does. 2.

scenes.title: 3.4 Fundamentals of Python Programming · 2
scenes.body: Indentation (spaces) — C++ and Java use curly brackets { } to mark a block of code (a group of statements that belong together). Python instead uses indentation : spaces at the beginning of a line. Indentation is mandatory in Python. The standard is 4 spaces (or 1 tab). Reading the program line by line: Line 1 starts with # , so Python skips it. Line 2 prints Hello, World! . Line 3 asks a question: is 5 greater than 2? The colon : says "a block follows". Line 4 is a comment inside the block (ignored).

scenes.title: 3.4 Fundamentals of Python Programming · 3
scenes.body: Line 5 is indented by 4 spaces, so it belongs to the if block. Because 5 > 2 is true, it runs. What happens if you forget the indentation? scenes.title: 3.5 Control Structures
scenes.body: Control structures decide the order in which statements are executed in a program (the "flow of control"). Almost every program is built from just three basic structures: Sequence — do the steps one after another, top to bottom. Selection — choose a path depending on a condition ( if , else ). Repetition — repeat steps (loops: for , while ). Morning routine as control structures: Sequence: wake up → brush teeth → have breakfast. Selection: if it is raining, take an umbrella; else take a cap.

scenes.title: 3.5.2 Selection Statements: if and if-else
scenes.body: Selection changes the flow of a program based on a condition — an expression that is either True or False. It helps a program respond intelligently to different situations. 1. The if statement executes a block of code only if the condition is True. If the condition is False, the block is completely skipped. 2. The if-else statement provides two paths : if the condition is true, do this; else (otherwise), do that. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

scenes.title: 3.5.3 Repetition Statements: the for Loop and range()
scenes.body: A repetition statement (loop) lets a block of code run again and again . This greatly reduces the need to write the same code many times. Each single run of the loop body is called an iteration . 1. The for loop is used when the exact number of iterations is known . It takes each value from a sequence one by one and stores it in the loop variable (e.g. i ). The range() function generates the sequence of numbers for the loop: You can see all the values of a range at once by converting it to a list.

scenes.body: 2. The while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains True . It is used when the exact number of iterations is not known in advance (for example, "keep asking until the password is correct"). A while loop needs three parts: (1) initialise a variable before the loop, (2) test the condition, (3) update the variable inside the loop. If you forget the update, the condition never becomes False and the loop never stops — an infinite loop .

scenes.title: 3.5.3 Nested Loops and for vs while
scenes.body: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely, from start to finish, for every single iteration of the outer loop . If the outer loop runs 2 times and the inner loop runs 3 times, the inner body runs 2 × 3 = 6 times. A star triangle. The outer loop chooses the row; the inner loop prints that many stars on the same line ( end="" ), and the empty print() moves to the next line. Row 1: inner loop runs once → * . Row 2: twice → ** . And so on up to row 4.

scenes.title: 3.6 Libraries in Python
scenes.body: A library (also called a module ) is a collection of pre-written code that offers ready-made functions. Instead of writing a square-root algorithm from scratch, you import math and call math.sqrt() . Libraries save time, reduce bugs and let you stand on other programmers' work. There are five common ways to import a library. Method 3 (import only what you need) is the best habit: it is clearer and uses less memory than from math import * .

scenes.title: 3.7 Debugging Code in Python
scenes.body: Debugging is the process of identifying, tracing and fixing bugs so a program works correctly. Every program you write will have bugs. The skill is not "never make a mistake"; it is "find the mistake quickly". Python errors fall into three families: Reading a traceback. When Python crashes it prints a roadmap: the file, the line number, and the error type. Diagnosis: on line 1 we tried to convert the letters "abc" into an integer, which raised a ValueError . Examiners love "identify the error type" questions.

scenes.title: 3.7 Debugging Code in Python · 2
scenes.body: Ask: (1) Does it refuse to start? → syntax. (2) Does it crash mid-run? → runtime. (3) Does it run but give a wrong answer? → logical. Write the name of the error and how to fix it. Fix syntax errors first (the program cannot start). Then run it. Then check the output against a hand-worked example to catch logical errors. A logical error is the most dangerous because Python reports nothing. Always test with values whose answer you already know (for a rectangle 3 by 4, area must be 12, not 7). 1.

scenes.title: Data and Analysis
scenes.body: Chapter 4 This chapter teaches you how raw facts become organised information in a database, how tables are linked with keys, how to draw an ER diagram, and how to build tables, forms, queries and charts in Microsoft Access. scenes.title: 4.1.1 Data, Information and Database
scenes.body: Data are unprocessed facts, figures or observations. They can be quantitative (numbers: 80, 75, 90) or qualitative (descriptions: the colours of cars in a parking lot). Data on its own is not very useful — a list of marks does not yet tell you whether the class is strong. When you organise, process and interpret data, it becomes information . Information has meaning and supports a decision.

scenes.title: 4.1.2 Database Management System (DBMS)
scenes.body: A DBMS is software that lets you create, manage and interact with databases. It sits between the user and the stored files. You never edit raw data files by hand — you talk to the DBMS (Access, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite) and it handles storage, security and consistency. Advantages you must be able to list: Less redundancy. The department name is stored once, not in every student row. Consistency. Change a phone number once; every screen that uses it shows the new number. Security.

scenes.title: 4.2 Database Components (Tables, Records, Fields)
scenes.body: The basic structure is a table (also called a relation): rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, holding facts about one kind of thing (Students, Teachers, Books). A record (row, tuple) is one complete instance — everything about Ali. A field (column, attribute) is one kind of fact — the whole Name column, or the whole Grade column. The row 101 | Ali | CS | A is one record . The Name column is one field . Memory: row = record = one person. column = field = one question on the admission form.

scenes.title: 4.3.1 Keys and Integrity Constraints
scenes.body: A key is a field (or a set of fields) that uniquely identifies records and links tables. Integrity constraints are the rules that keep those keys honest. Candidate key. Any field (or combination) that could uniquely identify a row. A table may have several. In an Employee table: EmpID, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport are all candidate keys. Primary key (PK). The one candidate you actually choose. Rules: unique, never NULL, only one PK per table (it may be a composite of two columns). Example: EmpID. Alternate key.
scenes.urdu: کینڈیڈیٹ کی وہ فیلڈ ہے جو ریکارڈ کی شناخت کر سکے۔ پرائمری کی منتخب شدہ شناخت ہے — منفرد اور خالی نہیں۔ جو بچ جائیں وہ آلٹرنیٹ کیز ہیں۔ فارن کی دوسرے ٹیبل کی پرائمری کی کی طرف اشارہ کرتی ہے اور ٹیبلز کو جوڑتی ہے۔

The one candidate you actually choose. Rules: unique, never NULL, only one PK per table (it may be a composite of two columns). Example: EmpID. Alternate key.

scenes.title: 4.3.1 Keys and Integrity Constraints · 2
scenes.body: The leftover candidate keys. After EmpID is chosen, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport become alternate keys — still unique, just not “the” identifier. Foreign key (FK). A field in this table that refers to the PK of another table. It may contain duplicates (many employees in one department) and, in some designs, NULL. Classroom analogy. Roll Number, B-Form number and phone number can all identify a student (candidate keys). The school picks Roll Number as the primary key. B-Form and phone become alternate keys.

A phone number is a bad PK: people change numbers, two siblings may share one, and some students have none (NULL). Roll numbers are issued by the school and stay unique. 1. scenes.title: 4.3 Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)
scenes.body: An RDBMS stores data in several tables and uses primary and foreign keys to keep relationships. Banks, universities and NADRA use RDBMS software. Extra strengths on top of a plain DBMS: Reduces redundancy by splitting data into related tables. Supports many users at once, with permissions. Is queried with SQL (Structured Query Language) — a standard language of SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

scenes.title: 4.4 Entity Relationship Model (ER-Model)
scenes.body: The ER model is the architect’s blueprint: you draw what will be stored and how it connects before you create tables in Access. Three building blocks: Rectangle = entity, diamond = relationship, oval = attribute. Underline the primary-key attribute. Cardinality (types of relationship) The M:N rule. A relational database cannot store M:N directly — it duplicates data. Break it into two 1:M relationships with a junction table (also called a bridge or associative table). Example: Enrollment(StudentID, ClassID, Date).

scenes.title: 4.5 Referential Integrity
scenes.body: Referential integrity means every foreign-key value in a child table must match an existing primary-key value in the parent — or be NULL if the design allows it. It stops orphan records . If Result.StudentID is a FK to Student.StudentID, you cannot type Result for student 999 if 999 is not in Student. You also cannot delete student 101 while results for 101 still exist — unless you first handle those child rows. Parent — STUDENT Child — RESULT Cascade operations Cascade Update.

scenes.title: 4.5 Referential Integrity · 2
scenes.body: Change the PK in the parent, and every matching FK in the child changes automatically. Ali’s ID 101 → 201 updates Enrollments too. Nothing is left pointing at a vanished 101. Cascade Delete. Delete the parent, and related child rows are deleted too. If Sara (102) leaves school, her Enrolment and Result rows disappear. That prevents “ghost” marks for a student who is gone.

scenes.title: 4.6 Relational Schema Development
scenes.body: A relational schema is the formal written design of the database: table names, fields, primary keys, foreign keys and how tables relate. You write it before clicking around in Access. It defines (1) how data is split into tables, (2) which columns each table has, (3) which fields are PK/FK, (4) the relationships. Benefits: less redundancy, integrity planned in advance, easier to grow later. Written schema for a tiny college: Skipping the schema is like building a house without a drawing.

scenes.title: 4.7 Case Study — Library Management System
scenes.body: A college library needs a database. Walk the seven steps examiners expect. Step 1 — Requirements. A book has ID, title, author, publisher. A member (student/teacher) has ID, name, contact. A member can borrow many books; a book can be borrowed by different members over time. Record Issue Date and Return Date. Step 2 — Entities. Book, Member. (Borrowing will need a third entity in step 6.) Step 3 — Attributes. Book: BookID (PK), Title, Author, Publisher. Member: MemberID (PK), Name, ContactInfo.

scenes.body: Four objects you will meet in Access. Learn the one-line jobs cold: Store → Enter → Search → Print. Tables, Forms, Queries, Reports. scenes.title: 5.1 Introduction to Computing Impacts
scenes.body: Computing means using computers and computer-based devices to store, process and share information. Today computing is an important part of your daily life. You use computers, mobile phones, the internet and smart devices almost everywhere — at home, in college and on the road. In Pakistan, computing is becoming vital (very necessary) in: Schools and colleges — online admissions, e-books, online results of the Sindh boards. Hospitals — computerised patient records, digital X-rays, online appointment systems.

scenes.title: 5.1.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)
scenes.body: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human thinking, such as recognising faces, understanding language and making decisions. Understand the name in two parts: Artificial — it is created by humans ; it is not natural. Intelligence — it can perform tasks that require thinking . AI systems use data to make decisions . The more good data an AI system sees, the better it becomes at recognising patterns (repeating features) and predicting what to do.

scenes.title: 5.1.2 Internet of Things (IoT) & Components
scenes.body: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system in which physical devices are connected to the Internet and can collect and share data to perform tasks automatically . The "things" are ordinary objects — watches, cameras, cars, fans, water pumps — that have been given sensors and an internet connection so they can "talk" to each other and to us. Source example: A smartwatch collects your heart-rate data and sends it to your mobile phone, where it is displayed.

scenes.title: 5.1.2 Internet of Things (IoT) & Components · 2
scenes.body: Components of IoT systems IoT relies on six foundational components to work properly. Understanding each component Sensors turn something in the real world (heat, movement, a fingerprint, smoke, wetness of soil) into data. A smoke sensor in a Karachi shopping mall "smells" smoke and reports it. Actuators do the opposite: they take a digital command and make something move or change . The water valve that opens, the motor that turns, the door that slides open at a bank entrance. Connectivity is the "road" for data.

scenes.body: Data Analytics is the process of collecting, organising, cleaning, studying and presenting data to find useful information. It helps people make better decisions. Data means raw facts and figures (for example, "72, 45, 88"). Information is data that has been processed so it has meaning ("Ali scored 72%; he passed"). Data Analytics is the bridge from data to information. Source example: A college collects exam marks, calculates percentages, and identifies which students need extra help.

scenes.body: This entire process is Data Analytics. Components of Data Analytics Data Analytics comprises five key components , which happen in order like a pipeline: 1. Collection → 2. Storage → 3. Data Storage — Storing data safely and properly after collection. It can be stored in files, databases, spreadsheets or the cloud.

scenes.title: 5.1.3 Data Analytics & Components · 3
scenes.body: Data Cleaning — Identifying and correcting errors in data. Raw data may contain: Duplication of records (the same student entered twice), Incorrect values (typos, e.g. marks "870" instead of "87"), Missing files or records (a student's marks not entered), Improper formats (dates written as 05/10/2026 in one place and "5 Oct 26" in another). Data Analysis — Studying the clean data to identify patterns, trends and relevant information for problem-solving (e.g. finding out which subjects students failed the most).

scenes.title: 5.2 Uses of IoT in Different Areas
scenes.body: IoT improves efficiency (doing more with less effort), saves time , and enhances the overall quality of life . It plays a significant role in developing modern infrastructure (the basic systems of a country — roads, power, water, hospitals). The source lists six areas. 1. Examples: interviews, photographs, diaries, NADRA official records. 2. Secondary sources contain information that has already been collected and explained by someone else .

scenes.title: 5.4 Impacts of Computing in Various Fields
scenes.body: Computing has drastically changed society. It makes life faster and more connected , but it also brings challenges like privacy risks and technology addiction . For every field, think of both sides. Smart and responsible use Protect personal information and use strong passwords (long, with letters, numbers and symbols; never share your OTP or CNIC details with callers). Do not share fake news or unverified WhatsApp forwards. Balance screen time with physical sports and activities.

scenes.title: 5.5 Assistive Technologies
scenes.body: Assistive technologies are devices, software and systems that help people with disabilities or functional limitations (difficulty in seeing, hearing, moving, speaking, remembering, etc.). They allow more people to participate equally in school, work and society. There are four categories : Mobility · Sensory · Communication · Cognitive A screen reader is software that reads aloud the text on a screen, so a blind person can use a phone or computer. VoiceOver is Apple's screen reader; Android has TalkBack.

scenes.title: 5.5.1 Importance of Assistive Technologies
scenes.body: Assistive technologies are important for three main reasons: Equal access to education: Screen readers allow blind students to read digital textbooks equally with their peers (classmates). Independence in daily life: Mobility aids reduce the need for constant human assistance — a person in a smart wheelchair can go to the market without someone pushing. Social inclusion: They break down barriers, allowing individuals to work, study and socialise confidently.

scenes.title: 6.1 Introduction to Digital Literacy
scenes.body: Digital literacy is the ability to understand and use digital devices, the internet, and online tools in a safe , effective , and responsible manner. Look at the three key words: Safe – you protect yourself and others online (for example, you do not share passwords or private details). Effective – you get the job done well (for example, you find the right information quickly). Responsible – you use information honestly and fairly (for example, you do not copy someone else's work or spread false news).

When his teacher asks him to find the population of Karachi, he copies the first number he sees on a random website and does not check where it came from. Step 1 Can he use devices? Yes. He has basic skills. Step 2 Can he locate and judge information? No. He did not check whether the website was reliable. Step 3 Conclusion: Ali has computer skills but is not yet fully digitally literate .

scenes.title: 6.2 Digital Literacy in the Information Age
scenes.body: The Information Age is the period we live in now, where vast amounts of data are produced , shared and accessed instantly through the internet, mobile devices and digital platforms (websites, apps, social media). Simply having access to technology is not enough . Owning a smartphone does not make you good at using information. You must develop the skills to understand , manage and use information wisely. Digital literacy goes beyond basic computer skills.

scenes.title: 6.3 Types of Data
scenes.body: Data means facts, numbers, words or observations that we collect. The data gathered through a survey, an investigation or a classroom project can be described in two ways: qualitatively or quantitatively . Knowing the difference is critical, because each type is analysed in a different way. 6.3.1 Qualitative Data Qualitative data describes what people think, feel, notice or experience . It is non-numerical and descriptive : it is made of words, not numbers. The word comes from quality (what something is like).

Examples: number of students using the internet daily; marks obtained in a test; time spent online in hours.

scenes.title: 6.4 Data-Collection Strategies
scenes.body: Digital literacy is not limited to finding information that already exists on the internet. You should also learn how to gather original (new) information yourself. A data-collection strategy is a planned method for gathering this information. The five common strategies are: Interviews · Surveys · Prototypes · Observation · Simulations Mnemonic for the five strategies: "I S P O S" – " I S aw P eople O n S creens": Interviews, Surveys, Prototypes, Observation, Simulations.

scenes.title: 6.4.1 – 6.4.2 Interviews and Surveys
scenes.body: 6.4.1 Interviews An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person . It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group . Questions are planned in advance , so you do not forget anything important. Answers are usually qualitative (opinions, reasons, experiences). Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?"). Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people.
scenes.urdu: انٹرویو ایک منصوبہ بند گفتگو ہے جس میں کسی ایک فرد یا چھوٹے گروہ سے براہِ راست معلومات حاصل کی جاتی ہیں؛ اس کے جوابات عموماً کیفیتی ہوتے ہیں۔ سروے میں ایک ہی سوالات بہت سے لوگوں سے پوچھے جاتے ہیں، کاغذ پر یا گوگل فارمز (Google Forms) جیسے ڈیجیٹل ٹولز کے ذریعے، جو جوابات…

It may be on paper or created with digital tools such as Google Forms or Microsoft Forms . Note: online survey tools automatically collect responses and display basic charts , which makes data analysis much easier.

scenes.title: 6.4.3 – 6.4.5 Prototypes, Observation and Simulations
scenes.body: 6.4.3 Prototypes A prototype is a simple early version of a product, model or solution. It allows an idea to be tested before time and effort are spent on the final version. Users try the prototype and give feedback , and this feedback becomes useful data for improvement . Example: Before building a full school app, you draw the screens on paper (or make a few clickable screens in a design tool) and ask five classmates to try "finding the timetable". You note where they get confused.

scenes.title: 6.4.3 – 6.4.5 Prototypes, Observation and Simulations · 2
scenes.body: 6.4.4 Observation In observation , the researcher watches what people do or what happens in a situation and records the results carefully . No direct questions are asked. The data may be qualitative (written notes, e.g. "students push in the queue") or quantitative (counts, e.g. "42 students bought samosas in 10 minutes"). Why use it? People sometimes say one thing and do another. Observation shows what really happens. 6.4.5 Simulations A simulation is a computer-based model of a real situation .

scenes.body: Variables (the things that can change, like speed, temperature or number of people) can be changed to see what happens. Simulations are highly useful when real experiments are costly, risky or difficult to perform. Examples: a flight simulator for training pilots (real crashes are dangerous); a traffic simulation to test what happens if a new signal is added (changing real roads is costly); a weather model to predict a cyclone (you cannot experiment with real weather). Choosing the right method.

scenes.title: 6.5 Primary and Secondary Data
scenes.body: Whenever you use data, it is important to know where it came from . The source affects how much control the researcher had over collecting it, and how confidently the results can be used. 6.5.1 Primary Data Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher for a particular purpose . It is gathered directly from people, events or situations, rather than taken from an already published source. Sources: interviews, surveys, observations, experiments.
scenes.urdu: بنیادی ڈیٹا (Primary Data) محقق خود کسی خاص مقصد کے لیے براہِ راست جمع کرتا ہے، مثلاً سروے، انٹرویو یا مشاہدہ۔ ثانوی ڈیٹا (Secondary Data) پہلے ہی کسی اور نے جمع کیا ہوتا ہے اور اسے نئے مقصد کے لیے دوبارہ استعمال کیا جاتا ہے، جیسے کتابیں، رپورٹس اور آن لائن ڈیٹا بیس۔ بنیادی…

It is gathered directly from people, events or situations, rather than taken from an already published source. Sources: interviews, surveys, observations, experiments.

scenes.title: 6.5 Primary and Secondary Data · 2
scenes.body: 6.5.2 Secondary Data Secondary data has already been collected by someone else and is being used again for a new purpose . It is taken from existing archives (stored collections of information). Sources: books, research articles, official reports, web statistics, online databases. Primary data is collected by you; secondary data was collected by others. 6.5.3 Difference Between Primary and Secondary Data Primary or secondary? Hira is researching "Internet use among students in Hyderabad".

scenes.title: 6.6 Designing a Data-Collection Approach
scenes.body: Before collecting data, a researcher must have a plan . A plan makes sure that the information gathered is accurate , relevant (related to the question) and useful . Follow these eight steps in order: Define the research question clearly. What exactly do you want to find out? Decide the type of data needed: quantitative, qualitative, or both. Select suitable methods (survey, interview, observation). Choose the sample or target group – the people who will give you data.
scenes.urdu: ڈیٹا جمع کرنے سے پہلے منصوبہ بندی ضروری ہے: تحقیقی سوال واضح کریں، ڈیٹا کی قسم طے کریں، مناسب طریقہ چنیں، نمونہ (Sample) منتخب کریں، فارم اور سوالات تیار کریں، احتیاط سے ڈیٹا جمع کریں، اسے اسپریڈشیٹ میں محفوظ کر کے بیک اپ رکھیں، اور اخلاقیات کا خیال رکھیں۔ اجازت (Consent)…

scenes.title: 6.7 Presenting Data Using Digital Tools: 6.7.1 Spreadsheets and 6.7.2 Presentations
scenes.body: Collecting data is only one part of the work. You must also present your findings so that others can understand them quickly and easily . Digital tools make this much easier. The four main tools are spreadsheets, presentations, infographics and reports. 6.7.1 Spreadsheets Spreadsheets such as MS Excel , Google Sheets and Apple Numbers arrange information in rows (horizontal, numbered 1, 2, 3…) and columns (vertical, lettered A, B, C…).
scenes.urdu: ڈیٹا جمع کرنے کے بعد اسے پیش کرنا بھی ضروری ہے۔ اسپریڈشیٹ (جیسے ایکسل اور گوگل شیٹس) میں ڈیٹا قطاروں اور کالموں میں ترتیب دیا جاتا ہے، اور ‎=SUM()‎ اور ‎=AVERAGE()‎ جیسے فارمولوں سے مجموعہ، اوسط اور فیصد نکالے جاتے ہیں۔ پریزنٹیشن سافٹ ویئر (جیسے پاور پوائنٹ) میں مختصر نکات،…

scenes.title: 6.7 Presenting Data Using Digital Tools: 6.7.1 Spreadsheets and 6.7.2 Presentations · 2
scenes.body: The box where a row and column meet is a cell , named by its column and row, e.g. B2 . With a spreadsheet you can: Enter data systematically (one record per row). Calculate totals, averages and percentages. Sort (arrange in order) and filter (show only some rows) records. Create charts and graphs automatically. A formula always starts with = . A range such as B2:B4 means "cells B2 to B4". Analysing the case-study spreadsheet.

scenes.body: The data from the 6.8 case study (Step 8) is entered like this: Step 1 – Total hours: =SUM(B2:B4) → 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 . Step 2 – Average hours: =AVERAGE(B2:B4) → 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 hours (to 2 decimal places). Step 3 – Most and least: =MAX(B2:B4) → 5 ; =MIN(B2:B4) → 2 . Step 4 – Median: sorted values 2, 3, 5 → middle = 3 . =MEDIAN(B2:B4) gives 3. Step 5 – How many use the phone for study? =COUNTIF(C2:C4,"Yes") → 2 . Step 6 – Percentage: =COUNTIF(C2:C4,"Yes")/COUNTA(C2:C4) → 2 ÷ 3 = 0.667; format the cell as % → 66.7% .

scenes.title: 6.7.3 – 6.7.4 Infographics and Reports
scenes.body: 6.7.3 Infographics An infographic (information + graphic) is a visual way of presenting information, facts or data so that people can understand the main idea quickly and easily . Tools such as Canva , Power BI or Tableau can be used. A good infographic should: Simplify complex concepts. Highlight the most important findings and results. Use clear visuals , limited text and accurate information. 6.7.4 Reports Reports are structured documents used to present collected data, findings, analysis and conclusions.

scenes.title: 6.8 Case Study: Digital Inquiry Project
scenes.body: This case study shows how to apply all the ideas of this chapter to solve a real-world problem from start to finish. An inquiry is an investigation to find the answer to a question. Research question: "How does daily mobile phone use affect the study habits of students?" Scenario: Students notice classmates using phones during free periods and while studying. Some say phones help them learn; others say phones waste time . The class must investigate whether phone use helps or harms study habits.

scenes.body: Use the data only for educational purposes . Why "different sections" matters. Suppose the group surveyed only the 40 students of the Pre-Engineering section who sit in the front rows. Problem: these students might study more than average, so the results would show less phone distraction than is true for the whole class. Fix: pick students from every section (e.g. 10 each from Pre-Medical, Pre-Engineering, Computer Science and Commerce). Now the sample better represents all Class XI students.

scenes.body: The counts (12, 21, 7) are estimated from the bar heights in the source chart. Making the chart in Google Sheets. Step 1 – Count each group. If the hours are in B2:B41, use =COUNTIF(B2:B41,"<3") for under 3 hrs, =COUNTIFS(B2:B41,">=3",B2:B41,"<5") for 3 to under 5 hrs, and =COUNTIF(B2:B41,">=5") for 5 hrs or more. (This gives non-overlapping groups.) Step 2 – Check the total. 12 + 21 + 7 = 40 ✓ – every student is counted exactly once. Step 3 – Percentages. 12 ÷ 40 = 30%; 21 ÷ 40 = 52.5%; 7 ÷ 40 = 17.5%.

scenes.body: Step 10: Analyse the results To analyse means to study the data carefully to find patterns and trends . By looking at the spreadsheet and charts, the group identifies: Most students (the majority) use phones for 3–5 hours daily . Half use it for educational purposes (lectures/notes). A clear trend: students who use phones mostly for entertainment report much higher distraction levels than those who use them for study.

scenes.body: Set daily screen-time limits . Take physical breaks from screens to protect health. From numbers to a finding. Step 2: "Half use it for educational purposes" means about 20 of the 40 students chose Lectures or Notes as their main activity (20 ÷ 40 = 50%). Formula: =COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Lectures")+COUNTIF(D2:D41,"Notes") .

scenes.title: Computer Systems (HCI)
scenes.body: Chapter 1 This chapter teaches you Human-Computer Interaction (HCI): how people and computers talk to each other, how to design screens that are easy and fair to use, and how to test those designs before they go live. You will apply every idea to things you already use in Pakistan — a bank ATM, JazzCash, and a school portal.
scenes.speak: Chapter 1 This chapter teaches you Human-Computer Interaction (HCI): how people and computers talk to each other, how to design screens that are easy and fair to use, and how to test those designs before they go live. You will apply every idea to things you already use in Pakistan , a bank ATM, JazzCash, and a school portal.

scenes.title: 1.1 Fundamentals of Human-Computer Interaction
scenes.body: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is the study and design of technology so that it serves people . An HCI system is easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). The three names mean the same idea: the meeting point of a person and a machine. HCI is not only "making a pretty screen". It asks: Can a student in Hyderabad find results on the school portal in 30 seconds? Can a grandmother send JazzCash without help?

Haptics means physical feedback you can feel, such as a phone vibrating when a JazzCash payment succeeds.

scenes.title: 1.1.1 Traditional Interaction and 1.1.2 Natural Interaction
scenes.body: 1.1.1 Traditional interaction is the basic way people use everyday devices. It relies on standard input and output: a mouse, a keyboard, a keypad, a monitor, speakers, or a simple touchscreen tap and swipe. Computer: moving a mouse and typing on a keyboard; output via monitor and speakers. Smartphone (traditional use): tapping and swiping on a touchscreen; output via screen lighting and vibrations. 1.1.2 Natural interaction is advanced, smart technology that lets people interact without a mouse or keyboard .

scenes.title: 1.2 Applications of HCI (Domains of Life)
scenes.body: HCI is used to design and develop interactive systems such as desktop applications, websites and mobile apps . These are human-centred solutions built to meet user needs across many domains of life. A domain is an area of daily activity — health, money, school, talking to people. When you design for a domain, you design for that domain's users, tasks and risks . A mistake on a games app is annoying. A mistake on a medical or banking screen can harm a person or lose money.

scenes.title: 1.3 Components of HCI
scenes.body: HCI relies on several primary components that work together. If one component is weak, the whole interaction feels broken. The first four are the people, the machine, the conversation, and the job to be done. The user performs a task through interaction with a computer system. All four parts must fit together. Worked example: label the four components of an HBL ATM withdrawal. User: end user = the account holder standing at the machine; stakeholder = the bank that owns the ATM and must keep it safe and working.

scenes.title: 1.3 Components of HCI · 2
scenes.body: Computer system: the ATM hardware plus the bank's software; it takes PIN input, shows a screen, and dispenses notes (output and feedback). User interaction: insert card → type PIN → choose "Cash" → type amount → confirm. Intent ("I want Rs 5,000") becomes a machine response (cash + receipt). Task: withdraw cash. Complexity: low (a few buttons). User knowledge: basic (PIN and amounts). Time: about one minute — much shorter than an online passport application. U-C-I-T: User, Computer system, Interaction, Task.

scenes.title: Types of User Interaction
scenes.body: User interaction can happen in many different ways depending on the technology used. Learn every type with one clean example — board questions often ask you to "list and explain" five or more. Worked example: a full JazzCash "Send Money" session, labelled by type. Open the app with a fingerprint → biometric . Home screen shows Send Money, Bill Payment, Load → you tap Send Money → menu-driven . Type the receiver's mobile number and the amount → form fill . The keypad vibrates on each tap → haptic .

scenes.body: vii) Feedback Feedback is the signal or response given to confirm or guide actions. scenes.title: 1.4 Importance of HCI
scenes.body: HCI ensures that machines are approachable and usable, turning complex technology into everyday tools. Good design makes technology simple and enjoyable (touchscreens). Poor design causes confusion and risks (unclear buttons on medical devices). This is why HCI is not optional decoration. A confusing JazzCash confirm button can send money to the wrong number. A confusing school-portal "Submit" can lock a student out of an online exam.
scenes.urdu: اچھا ایچ سی آئی پیچیدہ ٹیکنالوجی کو روزمرہ کا آسان اوزار بناتا ہے؛ برا ڈیزائن الجھن اور خطرہ پیدا کرتا ہے، جیسے طبی آلے پر غیر واضح بٹن۔ پانچ مضمرات: پیداوری بڑھتی ہے، شمولیت آتی ہے، جدت اپنائی جاتی ہے، معیشت مضبوط ہوتی ہے، اور رازداری و انصاف کی اخلاقی ذمہ داری پوری ہوتی ہے۔

scenes.body: Importance questions in the board exam expect the five implications below, each with a sentence of explanation. Worked example: good vs poor HCI, same task. Result: fast, few mistakes, the user trusts the app (productivity + economic loyalty + ethics of clear consent).

scenes.title: 1.5 Accessibility Principles
scenes.body: Accessibility principles are HCI guidelines that ensure digital systems are usable by all individuals, including people with diverse physical, sensory and cognitive abilities. They remove barriers to create equal access. Accessibility is not a "special extra". It is how you make sure a student with low vision, a shopkeeper who cannot use a mouse, or a colour-blind driver can still complete the task. Worked example: audit a school portal against the five principles. Contrast: are result PDFs pale grey on white?

scenes.title: 1.6 Need Analysis for Interface Design
scenes.body: Need analysis is the process of identifying the gap between the existing situation and the desired outcome . In HCI it is done before designing a UI, so that you understand users' goals, tasks, abilities and expectations. If you skip need analysis, you guess. Guessing is how a school portal ends up with 40 menus and no "Download date sheet" button on the home screen. Steps in need analysis: 1. Identify the users → 2. Collect information → 3. Analyse needs → 4. Prioritise → 5.

scenes.title: 1.7 Human-Computer Interaction Problems
scenes.body: HCI problems are common difficulties that stop users from using technology smoothly. They happen when systems fail to meet human needs or cognitive limits. Cognitive limits means the mind can only hold and process so much at once — if an app asks you to remember three SMS codes at the same time, it has gone past that limit. Board answers score well when you name the problem, explain it in one line, and give a concrete example (the source examples are safe; a matching local example is even better).
scenes.urdu: ایچ سی آئی مسائل وہ رکاوٹیں ہیں جو سسٹم کو انسانی ضرورت یا ذہنی حد کے مطابق نہ ہونے پر پیدا ہوتی ہیں۔ آٹھ مسائل: انٹرفیس کی پیچیدگی، کمزور فیڈبیک، عدم مطابقت (ایک جیسا نہ ہونا)، رسائی کی کمی، آلہ/براؤزر سے ناسازگاری، سیاق کو نظرانداز کرنا، زیادہ ذہنی بوجھ، اور اعتماد کی کمی…

scenes.body: Worked example: diagnose three local systems. ATM: six tiny unmarked buttons beside the screen and no "Cash is coming" message → interface complexity + poor feedback. A user walks away while cash is still coming out. JazzCash: "Send" is green on the home screen but orange on the confirm screen, and there is no padlock on the payment page → inconsistency + trust deficiency.

scenes.title: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI
scenes.body: Once you can name an HCI problem, you fix it with a matching method. The source lists eight methods. Learn each with its tiny example — they pair almost one-to-one with Section 1.7. Enhance usability: simplify navigation (a clear "Buy Now" button). Strengthen accessibility: support disabilities (captions on videos). Ensure consistency: keep layouts uniform (the same "Save" button everywhere). Provide clear feedback: show action results ("Payment Successful" popup).
scenes.urdu: ایچ سی آئی بہتر بنانے کے طریقے: نیویگیشن آسان کرنا، رسائی بڑھانا (کیپشن)، ایک جیسا لے آؤٹ، واضح فیڈبیک ("ادائیگی کامیاب")، ریسپانسیو ڈیزائن، صارف مرکز ڈیزائن (UCD) اور پائلٹ ٹیسٹ، ملٹی موڈل ان پٹ، اور مسلسل جانچ۔ ہر مسئلے کا ایک جوڑی دار حل یاد رکھیں۔

scenes.title: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI · 2
scenes.body: Improve adaptability: responsive design (the website scales to mobile screens). Apply user-centred design (UCD): focus on real user goals and pilot-test. Use multimodal interaction: allow touch, voice or gesture inputs combined. Continuous testing: regularly update based on user feedback. User-centred design (UCD) means the real user's goals drive every decision, and you trial (pilot-test) the design with those users instead of guessing in an office.

scenes.body: Responsive design means the layout rearranges itself for phone, tablet and PC, instead of staying a laptop-only page. Worked example: match each JazzCash / portal problem to a fix. One input only ↔ multimodal. Launch and forget ↔ continuous testing.

scenes.title: 1.9 User Interface Design (UI vs UX)
scenes.body: UI design is the process of creating and organizing the visual elements of a software application so users can interact with it easily and efficiently. 1.9.1 Components of a user interface 1.9.2 User experience (UX) UX is the overall experience a user has while interacting with a system — how smooth, comfortable and satisfying it feels. UI is what you see; UX is how it feels. Source example: food-delivery app. The UI is the nice pictures of burgers and the red buttons.

UI is what you see; UX is how it feels. Source example: food-delivery app. The UI is the nice pictures of burgers and the red buttons.

scenes.body: The UX is that the app loads fast, tracking works, and the food arrives without the user getting frustrated. Local walk-through: JazzCash. scenes.title: 1.9 User Interface Design (UI vs UX) · 3
scenes.body: UX = a student finds the chemistry practical date in under a minute on a phone, without calling the clerk. Pretty UI + slow, confusing flow = poor UX. Plain UI + fast, clear flow = good UX. Clothes vs day out. UI is the outfit (colours, buttons, icons). UX is the whole day (Did you arrive on time? Did you get wet? Were you stressed?). Examiners love the line: UI is what you see; UX is how it feels. Mistake: Writing "UI and UX are the same" or "UX is just colours".

scenes.title: 1.9.3–1.9.5 Wireframing, Figma and Prototypes
scenes.body: 1.9.3 Wireframing is creating a basic visual outline or blueprint of a user interface before the final design. It plans the structure without focusing on colours or detailed graphics. Low-fidelity wireframes (Lo-Fi) A simple black-and-white sketch showing basic layout (boxes and lines). Used early to test and share ideas quickly. Focuses purely on structure and flow. High-fidelity prototypes (Hi-Fi) A detailed version that looks almost exactly like the final product.
scenes.urdu: وائر فریم یو آئی کا بنیادی خاکہ ہے، رنگوں سے پہلے۔ لو فائی سیاہ و سفید ڈبے ہیں؛ ہائی فائی تقریباً حتمی شکل ہے، رنگ، فونٹ اور کلک ہونے والے بٹن کے ساتھ۔ فگما (Figma) مفت ویب ٹول ہے: فریم بناؤ، شکل اور متن ڈالو، فریم کاپی کرو۔ پروٹوٹائپ کوڈ سے پہلے کا چلنے والا نمونہ ہے جس میں…

scenes.title: 1.11 Test and Evaluate HCI (Evaluation Methods)
scenes.body: Testing checks if the product works properly (finding bugs). Evaluation determines whether it meets users' needs (usability). Together they improve the product before release. A school portal can be "bug-free" (testing passed) and still unusable if students cannot find the date sheet (evaluation failed). You need both. 1.11.1 Evaluation methods Heuristics are agreed rules of good design (for example "show system status", "be consistent").

Are labels consistent?). That is an expert review . After the portal is "finished", 30 students fill the 10 SUS questions.

scenes.body: A low score means it is still hard to use, even if there are no crashes. Ask: "On a scale of 0–10, would you recommend this portal to a friend in another college?" That is NPS (loyalty). scenes.title: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated)
scenes.body: Testing involves observing how the system behaves under specific conditions. Learn all seven methods. The three named in the heading — usability, A/B and automated — are the ones examiners ask most, but a complete answer also names the others. Usability testing: observing real users while they perform realistic tasks, to measure efficiency and satisfaction. If the user gets stuck, designers know where to fix the UI.
scenes.urdu: سات ٹیسٹنگ طریقے: یوزیبیلٹی (حقیقی صارف کو کام کرتے دیکھنا)، ٹاسک بیسڈ (وقت، کامیابی، غلطیاں ناپنا)، خودکار آڈٹ (بوت ٹوٹے لنک، سست رفتار، کم کنٹراسٹ ڈھونڈے)، اے/بی ٹیسٹ (آدھا صارف اے، آدھا بی؛ زیادہ کلک والا جیتے)، کمپیٹیبلٹی (براؤزر اور آلہ)، لوڈ ٹیسٹ (مثلاً دس ہزار لاگ…

scenes.title: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated) · 2
scenes.body: Task-based testing: assigning a specific task (for example, "Find a product and add it to cart") and strictly measuring completion time , success rate and number of errors . Automated audits: software bots scan websites to detect technical issues such as broken links, slow loading speeds or low colour contrast. A/B testing: comparing two versions of an interface (A and B). Half the users see A, half see B. The one with more clicks or sign-ups wins.

A/B testing: comparing two versions of an interface (A and B). Half the users see A, half see B. The one with more clicks or sign-ups wins.

scenes.title: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated) · 3
scenes.body: Compatibility testing: verifying the system on different browsers (Chrome, Safari), devices (mobiles, tablets, PCs) and operating systems. Performance and load testing: simulating high traffic (for example 10,000 users logging in at once) to see if speed drops or the server crashes. Keyboard and screen-reader walkthroughs: navigating using only the keyboard (Tab/Enter) or assistive technologies, to check accessibility for users with disabilities.

scenes.title: Career Opportunities in UI/UX
scenes.body: The same HCI skills you practised on ATMs, JazzCash and school portals are real jobs. Each role uses a different slice of this chapter. Worked example: who does which JazzCash task? "Interview shopkeepers about sending money" → UX designer . "Pick the green, the typeface and the Send button in Figma" → UI designer . "On Tap Send, slide to Confirm, then Success" → interaction designer . "Run SUS and an A/B test of two Send buttons" → usability researcher .

scenes.title: Computational Thinking & Algorithms
scenes.body: Chapter 2 Class XI taught you how to write algorithms. This chapter teaches you how to judge them: is the algorithm correct, clear and efficient? You will then learn the main data structures — array, linked list, stack, queue, tree and graph — so you can store data the smart way and trace how it is retrieved.

scenes.title: 2.1 Analyze algorithms for correctness
scenes.body: An algorithm is correct if its output matches the expected results for a given input. Analysing correctness means showing that the algorithm produces the intended output for all valid inputs , not just one lucky example. Two methods are used in this course: Trace tables → paper execution, line by line → Stepwise reasoning → logic blocks, overall state You already met the idea of a dry run in Class XI. Here you learn to do it formally, and to choose the method that fits the size of the algorithm.

scenes.title: 2.1 Analyze algorithms for correctness · 2
scenes.body: Worked example: what “correct” means. An algorithm is supposed to count how many of the heights 1.91, 2.01, 1.87, 1.57, 1.48 lie between 1.57 m and 1.91 m inclusive. Expected output: 3 (1.91, 1.87 and 1.57 qualify; 2.01 is too tall; 1.48 is too short). If a program prints 4, it runs but it is not correct . Correctness is about the right answer, not about “no crash”. Remember: runs ≠ correct . A logical error still produces output — just the wrong output.

scenes.title: 2.1.1 Trace Tables
scenes.body: A trace table is a technique used to monitor how the values of variables change during the execution of an algorithm. It is a paper execution of the code — a manual walkthrough, also called a dry run . You act as the computer and fill in one row after another. Purpose of trace tables Dry running: execute the algorithm line by line by hand. Debugging: find logical errors where the algorithm runs but the output is wrong. Validation: check that the algorithm does what it is intended to do.
scenes.urdu: ٹریس ٹیبل الگورتھم کا کاغذی اجرا (Dry Run) ہے۔ ہر قطار میں لکیر نمبر، متغیرات کی نئی قیمتیں، ان پٹ/آؤٹ پٹ اور شرط کا نتیجہ (True/False) لکھا جاتا ہے۔ فوجیوں کی مثال میں قد 1.57 سے 1.91 میٹر تک ہونا چاہیے، حدود سمیت؛ پانچ قدوں میں سے تین اہل ہیں اس لیے آؤٹ پٹ 3 ہے۔

scenes.title: 2.1.1 Trace Tables · 2
scenes.body: Components of a trace table Line / step number — which line is being executed. Variables — one column for every variable. Input / output — user inputs and printed results. Condition check — True/False for IF, WHILE, FOR, and similar tests. Worked example: soldiers who meet the height rule. To qualify for training, a soldier’s height must be between 1.57 and 1.91 metres, inclusive . Inputs: all soldiers’ heights. Output: the count of eligible soldiers.

scenes.title: 2.1.2 Stepwise Reasoning
scenes.body: Stepwise reasoning (also called logic verification ) breaks an algorithm into logical sections and checks the state of the algorithm at each stage. A state is a snapshot of what is true about the variables at that moment (for example, “Sum currently holds the total of the numbers seen so far”). You do not fill a row for every line. You think through the logic: Analyse each step of the algorithm. Check: does it start in a valid state ? Does it handle all possible cases ? Are the conditions correct ?
scenes.urdu: مرحلہ وار استدلال میں الگورتھم کو منطقی حصوں میں توڑ کر ہر مرحلے پر اس کی حالت (State) دیکھی جاتی ہے: کیا شروع درست ہے، کیا تمام صورتیں سنبھلی ہیں، کیا شرط صحیح ہے، اور کیا لوپ کے ہر چکر کے بعد بھی نتیجہ درست رہتا ہے۔ ایک سے N تک جمع کی مثال میں Sum شروع میں 0 ہے، لوپ 1 سے N…

scenes.title: 2.1.2 Stepwise Reasoning · 2
scenes.body: If the loop is correct at the start of an iteration, does it remain correct at the end ? Worked example: sum of the numbers from 1 to N. Step 1: Start Step 2: Input N Step 3: SET Sum = 0 Step 4: For i = 1 to N Step 5: Sum = Sum + i Step 6: END For Step 7: Print Sum Step 8: End Stepwise reasoning breakdown Think of stepwise reasoning as a teacher checking a proof , not as a cashier counting coins one by one. You ask “is this block always true?” instead of “what is Sum when i = 17?”.

scenes.body: Mistake: rewriting the whole trace table and calling it stepwise reasoning. Fix: write short comments about state (start, loop, finish, edges). If you listed every i from 1 to 1000, you used the wrong method. 1. What other name is given to stepwise reasoning? 2. For the sum algorithm, why is Sum = 0 a valid start? 3. What happens when N = 0, and is that correct? Answers: 1. Logic verification. 2. Because no numbers have been added yet, so the running total should be zero. 3.

scenes.title: 2.1.3 Comparing Trace Tables and Stepwise Reasoning
scenes.body: Both methods verify correctness, but they fit different situations depending on the complexity and length of the algorithm. Trace tables zoom in on values; stepwise reasoning zooms out on design. Worked example: which method would you pick? A 12-line loop that adds five heights. Use a trace table . The loop is short, you are a beginner, and you need the exact Total. A billing system with 40 functions. Use stepwise reasoning . You cannot fill 10,000 rows.
scenes.urdu: ٹریس ٹیبل خرد بینی (Micro) سطح پر کام کرتا ہے: ہر لائن اور ہر قیمت۔ مرحلہ وار استدلال بڑی (Macro) سطح پر ڈیزائن اور حالت چیک کرتا ہے۔ چھوٹے لوپ اور مبتدیوں کے لیے ٹیبل بہتر ہے؛ ہزار بار چلنے والے لوپ یا بڑے سسٹم کے لیے استدلال بہتر ہے۔

scenes.title: 2.1.3 Comparing Trace Tables and Stepwise Reasoning · 2
scenes.body: You check each module’s start state, end state and edge cases. A loop from i = 1 to 1,000 that should produce Sum = 500500. Do not write 1,000 rows. Argue: “Sum starts at 0; each i is added once; final Sum = n(n+1)/2 = 1000×1001/2 = 500500.” That is stepwise reasoning. Then dry-run a tiny N (say 5) with a trace table if you want extra confidence. Micro vs macro. Trace table = microscope (every cell). Stepwise reasoning = map (whole city). Beginners start with the microscope; designers need the map.

For “explain why the algorithm is correct for any N”, write stepwise reasoning. Differentiate questions are almost guaranteed: “Compare a trace table with stepwise reasoning.” Write a four-row table (best for, effort, primary goal, micro/macro). Add one sentence of advice: table for small loops and exact values; reasoning for large systems and proofs.

scenes.title: 2.2 Evaluating the Clarity of an Algorithm
scenes.body: Clarity means an algorithm is easy to read, understand and modify . In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster. A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time. The two key aspects of clarity are: Clarity → Modularity (parts) → Readability (text and flow) Worked example: speed versus clarity. Algorithm A finds the class average in 8 confusing lines with variables a , b , c .
scenes.urdu: وضاحت (Clarity) کا مطلب ہے الگورتھم پڑھنا، سمجھنا اور بدلنا آسان ہو۔ بہت سی صورتوں میں وضاحت رفتار سے بھی اہم ہے۔ اس کے دو حصے ہیں: ماڈیولریٹی (Modularity) یعنی کام کو حصوں میں بانٹنا، اور پڑھائی پن (Readability) یعنی متن اور بہاؤ صاف ہونا۔
