scenes.title: 2.2.1 Modularity
scenes.body: Modularity means breaking an algorithm into smaller, independent parts such as functions, classes or modules . This makes the algorithm more organised and easier to work with. How to evaluate modularity Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Each module should focus on one specific task. If a function calculates a sum, prints a report and saves a file, it violates SRP. Coupling. Modules should be reusable in different contexts. Good modularity means loose coupling : a change in one part does not smash the others.
scenes.urdu: ماڈیولریٹی کا مطلب الگورتھم کو آزاد حصوں (فنکشن، کلاس، ماڈیول) میں توڑنا ہے۔ جانچ کے تین اصول: واحد ذمہ داری (SRP) یعنی ایک فنکشن ایک کام؛ ڈھیلی جڑت (Loose Coupling) تاکہ ایک حصہ بدلنے سے دوسرے نہ ٹوٹیں؛ اور تجرید (Abstraction) یعنی اندرونی تفصیل چھپا کر صرف کام منگوانا، جیسے…
scenes.speak: Modularity means breaking an algorithm into smaller, independent parts such as functions, classes or modules . This makes the algorithm more organised and easier to work with. How to evaluate modularity Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). Each module should focus on one specific task. If a function calculates a sum, prints a report and saves a file, it violates SRP. Coupling. Modules should be reusable in different contexts. Good modularity means loose coupling : a change in one part does not smash the others.

scenes.title: 2.2.1 Modularity · 2
scenes.body: Tight coupling is when two functions share so many hidden details that you cannot reuse one without the other. Abstraction. A well-designed algorithm hides complex implementation details. You can call a sorting function without knowing whether it uses Bubble Sort or Selection Sort inside. Worked example: average of an array. Poor modularity (monoblock) All logic sits in one block, so you cannot reuse the sum.

scenes.title: 2.2.2 Readability
scenes.body: Readability is how easily another person can understand the purpose and logic of an algorithm without running it . It is about how clear the text and the flow are. How to evaluate readability Naming conventions — consistent rules for names. Good names make an algorithm easier to search and understand. Bad: v = d / t Good: velocity = distance / time Self-documentation — the algorithm explains itself, so you need fewer comments. Meaningful names and clean formatting make the purpose obvious.
scenes.urdu: پڑھائی پن یہ ہے کہ دوسرا شخص الگورتھم چلائے بغیر اس کا مقصد سمجھ لے۔ اچھے نام ( velocity = distance / time )، خود بیان (کم تبصرے)، سادہ کنٹرول فلو (گہری IF کے بغیر) اور ایک جیسا انداز (indentation اور casing) اسے آسان بناتے ہیں۔

scenes.title: 2.3 Assess Algorithm Efficiency
scenes.body: Algorithm efficiency is measured in terms of time and space — how fast it runs and how much memory it uses. The key considerations for assessing efficiency are: Number of steps (described with Big O notation ). Number of conditions (IF decisions). Number of repetitions (loops). Time (speed) + Space (memory) → Efficiency Worked example: two ways to find a name in 1,000,000 sorted records. Linear search checks about 1,000,000 names in the worst case (time grows with n).

scenes.title: 2.3.1 Number of Steps (Big O Notation)
scenes.body: When we discuss efficiency we ask how performance changes as the input size n increases. Big O notation is a mathematical method used to describe how the running time (or memory) grows as n grows. We ignore small constants and keep the most important term: if an algorithm does 3n + 5 steps we write O(n). In computer science, log n almost always means log base 2 (how many times you can halve n until you reach 1). Five common classes The source stresses O(1), O(log n), O(n) and O(n²).

scenes.title: 2.3.1 Number of Steps (Big O Notation) · 2
scenes.body: O(n log n) is the class of efficient general-purpose sorts, so you should recognise it when a question says “better than Bubble Sort but more than linear”. Growth table (log is log 2 ) Each cell is the approximate number of operations for that n. Read down a column to see how fast that class explodes. From n = 8 to n = 1,000,000, O(1) does not move, O(log n) only goes from 3 to about 20, O(n) becomes a million, and O(n²) becomes a million million — which is why nested loops “fail for large datasets”. Same n = 16.

scenes.title: 2.3.2 Number of Conditions
scenes.body: Conditions (IF statements) are decision points. Every condition forces the CPU to evaluate True or False, so excessive branching reduces performance. Computational cost. Each IF is extra work, even if the rest of the algorithm is simple. Nested conditions. IF inside IF often means a brute-force approach. It hurts both readability and speed. Short-circuiting (the optimisation goal). Stop evaluating as soon as the result is known. In a logical AND, if the first part is False the second part is skipped.

scenes.title: 2.3.3 Number of Repetitions
scenes.body: Repetitions (loops) are the most significant factor in algorithm efficiency. The structure of the loop decides how time grows with n. Worked example: count the inner-body runs. One loop: 5. Nested loops: 25 = 5². For n = 1,000 that would be 1,000 versus 1,000,000. Find the deepest loop . One loop ≈ O(n). Loop inside a loop ≈ O(n²). A loop that halves n ≈ O(log n). Mistake: counting the word for and ignoring how the index moves. Fix: a loop while n > 1: n = n // 2 is logarithmic, even though it is still “a loop”. 1.

scenes.title: 2.3.4 The Efficiency Evaluation Framework
scenes.body: To evaluate an algorithm at a conceptual level, ask three questions: Does it scale? If n grows 10 times, does time jump 10 times (linear) or 100 times (quadratic)? Quadratic scaling fails for large datasets. What is the bottleneck? Focus on the most time-consuming section (usually the deepest loop) and try to improve that part. Is the cost worth it? A theoretically faster O(log n) algorithm can be too complex to code and maintain.

scenes.title: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency
scenes.body: Improving an algorithm means reviewing it step by step: simplifying logic, removing redundant work, and picking smart data structures. A clear algorithm is easier to follow; an efficient one wastes fewer steps. 2.4.1 Refinements for clarity Use meaningful names. Replace vague variables with descriptive ones. Bad: a = b / c . Good: average = totalSum / totalItems . Break into modules. Divide a massive block into functions, for example separating CalculateSum() from the printing logic.

scenes.title: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency · 2
scenes.body: Improve structure and indentation. Packed loops and IF statements confuse the reader. Spacing reduces mental effort. Add comments. Keep them short. Explain why something is done, not just what is happening, especially for tricky logic. 2.4.2 Refinements for efficiency Reduce unnecessary steps. In Bubble Sort, after the first pass the largest value has settled at the end. Ignore that sorted tail on the next pass by shrinking the inner loop, and you save comparisons. Use better algorithms.

scenes.title: 2.4 Refinements to improve clarity and efficiency · 3
scenes.body: Searching 1 million sorted records with Binary Search instead of Linear Search changes the time from seconds to milliseconds. Avoid re-computing values (memoization / caching). If a value never changes, compute it once outside the loop, store it, and reuse it. Use appropriate data structures. Direct access → array. Hierarchical data → tree. Do not force one structure everywhere. Worked example 1 — shrinking Bubble Sort’s inner loop (n = 5). A naive inner loop always runs n−1 = 4 times, for 4 passes: 16 comparisons.

scenes.title: 2.5 Concept of Data Structure
scenes.body: A data structure is a systematic way of organising, storing and managing data so that an algorithm can access, modify and process it efficiently. Real-life analogy. Books on a shelf are arranged in a set order, so you can find a title quickly. Files in folders are grouped on purpose. Data structures do the same job inside computer memory. 1. Linear data structures Elements stand in a strict sequence, one after another. Each element (except the first and last) has exactly one predecessor and one successor .

scenes.title: 2.5 Concept of Data Structure · 2
scenes.body: Examples: Array, Linked List, Stack, Queue. 2. Non-linear data structures Elements are connected in a hierarchy or a network. One element can connect to several others at the same time. Examples: Tree, Graph. Linear: a line of neighbours. Non-linear: a node with more than one connection. Worked example: classify each everyday picture. Students standing in a single assembly line → linear (each has one in front and one behind).

scenes.body: A family tree of grandparents, parents and children → non-linear (one parent, several children). Roads linking Karachi, Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana in many ways → non-linear (a network). scenes.title: 2.5.1 Linear Data Structures: Array
scenes.body: An array holds a collection of similar items (the same data type) placed next to each other in contiguous memory (one continuous block). Each item has a position number called an index , usually starting from 0 . Because the address of any cell can be calculated from the index, you can jump straight to it. That is direct access (also called random access), and it is O(1). Six integers in contiguous cells. Direct access: A[3] jumps to 90 without walking 23, 76 and 12. Worked example: read by index.

scenes.title: Linear Data Structures: Linked List
scenes.body: A linked list stores data as a chain. Unlike an array, the items are not one continuous block. Each separate piece is a node sitting somewhere in memory. Each node has two parts: the actual data ; a link (pointer) holding the memory address of the next node. The first node is pointed to by HEAD . The last node’s link is NULL (nowhere). To find an item you start at HEAD and follow links one by one — sequential access , O(n). Real-life example: browser history.

scenes.title: Linear Data Structures: Stack
scenes.body: A stack is a linear data structure that works on the LIFO principle: Last-In, First-Out . The last element added is the first one removed. You cannot pull an item from the bottom or the middle. PUSH — add an item to the top . POP — remove the item from the top . A TOP pointer always names the current top item. Real-life example: Undo in a text editor. Every action is piled on the stack; Undo POPs the most recent action first. Three PUSH operations. The TOP is Data 3, so the first POP returns Data 3.

You cannot pull an item from the bottom or the middle. PUSH , add an item to the top . POP , remove the item from the top . A TOP pointer always names the current top item. Real-life example: Undo in a text editor. Every action is piled on the stack; Undo POPs the most recent action first. Three PUSH operations. The TOP is Data 3, so the first POP returns Data 3.

Undo, Redo, Back button and function calls are all stacks. Mistake: POPing from the bottom, or mixing LIFO with FIFO. Fix: stack = plates (top only). Queue = ticket line (front leaves, rear joins).

scenes.title: Linear Data Structures: Queue
scenes.body: A queue organises data on the FIFO principle: First-In, First-Out . Whoever arrives first is served first. Order truly matters. ENQUEUE — add an element at the Rear (back). DEQUEUE — remove an element from the Front . Real-life example: several documents sent to a printer. The printer prints the first document received, then the next. Three jobs waiting. New jobs join at the rear; service always takes the front. Worked example: ENQUEUE / DEQUEUE trace. Start empty. ENQUEUE 55, 76, 90, then ENQUEUE D, then DEQUEUE.
scenes.urdu: کیو FIFO پر چلتی ہے: جو پہلے آیا وہ پہلے نکلے۔ پیچھے (Rear) شامل کرنا ENQUEUE، آگے (Front) سے ہٹانا DEQUEUE ہے۔ پرنٹر کی قطار: جو فائل پہلے بھیجی گئی وہ پہلے چھپے گی۔ پہلی DEQUEUE ہمیشہ سب سے پرانا عنصر نکالتی ہے۔

New jobs join at the rear; service always takes the front. Worked example: ENQUEUE / DEQUEUE trace. Start empty. ENQUEUE 55, 76, 90, then ENQUEUE D, then DEQUEUE.

If your first removal is D, you treated the queue as a stack.

scenes.title: 2.5.2 Non-Linear Data Structures: Tree
scenes.body: A tree organises data in a hierarchy . Everything branches out from a single starting point called the root . It creates a strict one-to-many (parent–child) relationship. That is an excellent way to show how roles flow in an organisation. Real-life examples: a family tree (grandparents → parents → children) and folders inside folders on a drive. College tree: one root (Principal), then parent–child branches. No child has two parents in this model. Worked example: name the relationships. Root: Principal.
scenes.urdu: ٹری ڈیٹا کو درجہ بندی (Hierarchy) میں رکھتی ہے جو ایک جڑ (Root) سے پھوٹتی ہے۔ تعلق والدین-بچہ (ایک سے کئی) ہوتا ہے، جیسے پرنسپل → ڈین → ایچ او ڈی، خاندانی شجرہ، یا فولڈر کے اندر فولڈر۔ دو جڑیں یا چکر ٹری کو گراف بنا دیتے ہیں۔
scenes.speak: A tree organises data in a hierarchy . Everything branches out from a single starting point called the root . It creates a strict one-to-many (parent child) relationship. College tree: one root (Principal), then parent child branches. No child has two parents in this model. Worked example: name the relationships. Root: Principal.

Mistake: drawing a tree with two roots, or with an arrow going back up to the Principal from HOD CS (a cycle).

scenes.title: Non-Linear Data Structures: Graph
scenes.body: A graph organises data when things connect in a flexible, complex way. Unlike a tree, there is no strict hierarchy : any node can connect to any other node. Nodes (vertices) — the items (cities, people). Edges — the connections (roads, friendships). Examples: Facebook friends; GPS mapping (the fastest route between two cities). Four vertices A, B, C, D. Edges can form a cycle (A–B–D–C–A). A tree cannot do that. Worked example: Karachi – Hyderabad – Sukkur – Larkana. Cities are vertices. Roads are edges.
scenes.urdu: گراف لچکدار روابط کے لیے ہے: کوئی سخت درجہ بندی نہیں، کوئی بھی نوڈ کسی سے جڑ سکتا ہے۔ نوڈز (Vertices) چیزیں ہیں، کنارے (Edges) تعلق۔ فیس بک دوست اور GPS نقشہ کلاسیکی مثالیں ہیں۔ چکر (Cycle) اور کئی راستے گراف کو ٹری سے الگ کرتے ہیں۔

Edges can form a cycle (A B D C A). A tree cannot do that. Worked example: Karachi Hyderabad Sukkur Larkana. Cities are vertices. Roads are edges.

scenes.title: Non-Linear Data Structures: Graph · 2
scenes.body: You can travel Karachi → Hyderabad → Sukkur or Karachi → Larkana → Sukkur. There is no single “root city”. That is a graph, and GPS uses it to pick a fast route. Tree ⊂ Graph in shape-talk: a tree is a special graph with one root and no cycles. If you need cycles or many-to-many links, say graph . Mistake: using a tree for GPS because “Hyderabad comes under Sindh”. Fix: administration can be a tree; roads are a graph because you can loop and take alternative paths. 1. scenes.title: 2.6 Identify data structures in problem scenarios
scenes.body: To pick a structure, first see how the data is organised. If each item has a clear “before and after”, it is linear . If it branches or connects to many items, it is non-linear . 2.6.1 Linear scenarios Storing student grades for a class → Array. You usually know how many students there are, and all grades are the same type. Indices give rapid lookup. Music playlist / browser history → Linked list. Every song knows what comes next. When one finishes, follow the pointer. Frequent insert/delete is cheap.

scenes.title: 2.7 Trace data retrieval in Array, List and Queue
scenes.body: Tracing data retrieval means following the step-by-step path of how an algorithm finds or accesses data. Array, linked list and queue are all linear, but the effort to find an item is very different because of how they are organised inside. 2.7.1 Retrieval in an array Every element has a fixed index from 0 to n−1 pointing at a spot in memory. If the algorithm already knows the index, it does not search: it jumps (direct access, O(1)). Array = [10, 50, 20, 70, 90, 30]. Direct access: Array[2] = 20.

scenes.title: Programming Fundamentals
scenes.body: Chapter 3 This chapter teaches you how Python stores collections of data, how you write reusable functions, and how you save information in files so it is still there after the program ends. You will build small programs — attendance, a word counter, a calculator, and a grade tracker — that you can type and run yourself.

You will build small programs , attendance, a word counter, a calculator, and a grade tracker , that you can type and run yourself.

scenes.title: 3.1 Data Structures in Python
scenes.body: A data structure is a way of organising values in a program so you can store them, find them and change them. Every useful program is built on data structures. Python gives you two layers: Primitive data structures — the basic types that hold one value. Examples: integers ( int ), floating-point numbers ( float ), and booleans ( bool ). Abstract data structures — higher-level containers built from primitive types so you can hold many values and run richer operations. Examples: lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries .

scenes.title: 3.1 Data Structures in Python · 2
scenes.body: Python has these four abstract structures built in. You do not install anything extra. That is why collecting marks, names or settings is simpler in Python than in many other languages. One value versus a collection. A student’s age is one integer. That student’s three test marks need a list. type() tells you which structure a value has. age is a primitive integer. marks is an abstract list that holds three integers together. Primitive = one piece. Abstract = a box of pieces.

scenes.title: 3.1.1 Lists (Ordered, Mutable, Methods)
scenes.body: A list is Python’s most versatile built-in data structure. It stores an ordered collection of items in a single variable. Lists are mutable (you can change them after you create them) and they are written with square brackets [] . Why use a list? One variable can hold thousands of values. You can mix types if you need to. You can add, remove and sort items as the program runs. List indexing (positive and negative) Each item sits in a numbered slot called an index . Numbering starts at 0 from the left.

scenes.title: 3.1.2 Tuples (Ordered, Immutable)
scenes.body: A tuple is an ordered collection that is immutable — once created, you cannot add, remove or replace items. Think of it as a read-only list . Tuples use parentheses () . Like lists, they allow duplicates, mixed types, and indexing from 0 (including negative indices). A list is an open box you can refill. A tuple is a sealed box you may only look into. Slicing a tuple returns a new tuple , not a list. Negative indexing and [::-1] work exactly as they do for lists.

scenes.title: 3.1.3 Sets (Unordered, Unique, Math Operations)
scenes.body: A set stores an unordered, unindexed collection of unique elements. It is inspired by mathematical sets. You write a set with curly braces {} . Duplicates are removed as soon as the set is created. Because there is no index, myset[0] is illegal. The set itself is mutable (you can add and remove items). Each item inside must be immutable (numbers, strings, tuples of immutables — not lists). The two 3s and two 2s collapse to one each. Do not depend on the printed order: a set is unordered.

scenes.title: 3.1.4 Dictionaries (Key-Value Pairs)
scenes.body: A dictionary stores data as key–value pairs . It works like a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key ) to find its meaning (the value ). Write a dictionary with curly braces, and put a colon between each key and value. Ordered (Python 3.7+): insertion order is kept. Mutable : you can add, change and delete pairs. Keys are unique : if you repeat a key, the last value silently overwrites the earlier one. Values may repeat. You never search a dictionary by position. You search by key.

scenes.title: 3.1.7 Activity: Word Frequency Counter
scenes.body: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence. This is a classic use of a dictionary plus .get() : the word is the key, the count is the value. Logic, step by step. sentence.split() cuts on spaces and gives ['python', 'is', 'easy', 'python', 'is', 'fun', 'python', 'is', 'powerful'] . For a new word, word_freq.get(word, 0) is 0, then you store 0 + 1 = 1. For a word already in the dictionary, .get(word, 0) returns the current count, then you add 1.

A local variable is created inside a function. It exists only while that function is running. The main program cannot read it. ii) Global scope. A global variable is created outside all functions. Any function may read it, and the main program can use it too. Local — the name is invisible outside. First the function prints 50.

If a file is missing or a disk fails, the user should see a calm sentence such as “Please check the file name” or “Please try again later.” try = attempt; except = backup plan. scenes.title: 5.1 Machine Learning, Neural Networks and Deep Learning
scenes.body: Machine learning (ML) , neural networks (NN) and deep learning (DL) are important areas of artificial intelligence (AI) . AI is the broad field in which computers perform tasks that normally need human thinking, such as recognising a face, understanding speech or making a decision. These technologies help computers learn from data and make useful decisions without being explicitly programmed for every single step . You do not write a separate rule for every possible face or every Urdu accent.

scenes.title: 5.1.1 Machine Learning (ML)
scenes.body: A machine learning model is the system that learns from data and gives an output . Think of it as the trained brain of a computer program. In ordinary programming you write every rule yourself: if marks ≥ 40 then “Pass” . In machine learning you do not list every rule . You give the model many examples (data), it finds the patterns, and later it decides about new cases it has never seen. How it works — three steps: 1. Data input → 2. Learning (find patterns) → 3. Prediction on new data Data input.

scenes.title: 5.1.2 Neural Networks (NN)
scenes.body: A neural network is a computer model that learns patterns from data . It is directly inspired by the human brain , but it works as a mathematical computer system — not as living tissue. Your brain has billions of nerve cells ( neurons ) that pass signals to each other. A neural network copies this idea with small processing units also called neurons or nodes . These nodes are connected and pass information from one layer to another , performing calculations at each step.

scenes.body: A typical neural network has three kinds of layer: Input layer — receives the raw data (pixels of a face, samples of a sound, marks of a student). Hidden layer(s) — the “thinking” in the middle. Nodes here combine the inputs and learn features (eye distance, nose shape, an edge in a photo). Output layer — gives the final answer (unlock / keep locked; “this is a cat”; “pass / fail”). Input layer → Hidden layer(s) → Output layer Practical example from the source: face unlock. Step 1 — Input layer.

scenes.title: 5.1.3 Deep Learning (DL)
scenes.body: Deep learning is a machine-learning method in which computers use multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data. The word “deep” is used because data passes through several hidden layers before the system produces the final output. Each layer learns a different level of detail : Early layers learn simple features — edges, shapes, colours. Deeper layers combine those simple features to understand complex patterns — a whole face, or a specific car model (a Cultus versus a Corolla).

scenes.title: 5.1.4 Components of Neural Networks
scenes.body: The components of a neural network can be understood through its layered architecture . Data enters , gets processed , and exits , with mathematical adjustments happening inside. What happens inside one neuron Each neuron does a short calculation: Multiply each input x by its weight w . Add those products together, then add the bias b . This total is the weighted sum s . Pass s through an activation function .

scenes.title: 5.1.4 Components of Neural Networks · 2
scenes.body: A simple exam-friendly gate is a threshold (step) function : if s is at least the threshold, the neuron fires (output = 1); otherwise output = 0. In symbols: s = (x1 × w1) + (x2 × w2) + … + b , then y = 1 if s ≥ threshold , else y = 0 . One neuron: inputs × weights are summed, bias is added, then an activation function decides the output y. A small neural network: 3 input nodes, 4 hidden nodes, 2 output nodes. Each line is a weighted connection. Worked example: neuron calculation with numbers.

scenes.title: 5.1.4 Components of Neural Networks · 3
scenes.body: A college in Larkana uses a tiny network to guess whether a student is ready for a test. One hidden neuron receives two inputs: Step 1 — weighted products. x1 × w1 = 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.32 x2 × w2 = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.30 Step 2 — add bias to get the weighted sum s. s = 0.32 + 0.30 + 0.1 = 0.72 Step 3 — activation (threshold 0.5). Is 0.72 ≥ 0.5? Yes , so the neuron fires: y = 1 (ready for the test).

scenes.title: 5.1.5 Components of Deep Learning
scenes.body: Deep learning relies on specific advanced components to achieve its high accuracy. These components differentiate it from basic machine learning . A GPU was originally made for video games’ graphics, but it can do thousands of small multiplications in parallel — exactly what deep networks need. An epoch is one full pass through the training data. Ten epochs means the model has seen every training example ten times, adjusting weights a little each time.
scenes.urdu: ڈیپ لرننگ کو عام مشین لرننگ سے یہ چیزیں الگ کرتی ہیں: بہت بڑا ڈیٹا، بہت سی پوشیدہ تہیں، خود بخود خصوصیات نکالنا، سیکھنے کا الگورتھم جیسے بیک پروپیگیشن (Backpropagation)، طاقتور ہارڈویئر جیسا کہ جی پی یو (GPU)، اور بار بار تربیت جسے ایپوک (Epoch) کہتے ہیں۔

scenes.title: Future of AI, NN and DL in Pakistan
scenes.body: Machine learning, neural networks and deep learning will play a key role in Pakistan’s future. The National AI Policy 2025 highlights how artificial intelligence is now part of national planning, focusing on innovation, skill-building, ethical use and digital growth . To benefit from this future, Pakistan needs skilled individuals. You should focus on programming (such as Python) , mathematics , data analysis , problem-solving and the ethical use of technology .

scenes.body: Digital tools allow people to share files, attend online classes, edit documents and work together from different locations . Collaboration is useful only when data is protected and communication remains safe . Secure collaboration means using digital tools to work together in a safe, controlled and responsible way. scenes.body: Common methods: Username and password PIN (a short number code) OTP — One-Time Password , a code that works only once, usually sent by SMS or an authenticator app Biometrics — fingerprint or face Source example: a banking app sending an OTP to your phone before login . scenes.body: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means the system asks for two or more different factors before it trusts you. Two-factor authentication (2FA) is the common case of MFA that uses exactly two factors — usually password + OTP. If a thief in another city steals only your password, MFA still blocks them because they do not have your phone (or your fingerprint). ii) Access control Access control decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do : View, Edit, Comment, Download, Share.

scenes.title: 5.3.2 Data Protection (Encryption, Passwords, Backup, Firewall)
scenes.body: Data protection means keeping digital information safe from unauthorised access, misuse, loss, damage or accidental deletion . 1. Data encryption Encryption changes readable data ( plaintext ) into a coded form called ciphertext . Unauthorised users cannot understand ciphertext without the key. Symmetric encryption — the same key is used to encrypt and to decrypt. Asymmetric encryption — two keys : a public key to encrypt, a private key to decrypt.

scenes.body: A simple exam cipher is the Caesar cipher (a symmetric substitution cipher). You shift every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet. Shift 3 is the classic key: A → D, B → E, …, Z → C (the alphabet wraps around). 2. Strong passwords A strong password includes uppercase, lowercase, numbers and symbols . It resists brute-force guessing (trying every possible combination). Source example: Zk@2026#Pass . Weak: ahmed123 , pakistan , sindh , your date of birth.

The 3-2-1 backup rule is a practical standard: 3 copies of the data (the original plus two backups). 2 different types of storage media (for example laptop disk + USB, or disk + cloud).

scenes.title: 5.4.1 Common Security Threats (Malware, Phishing, DoS)
scenes.body: A security threat is any action, event or weakness that can harm a computer system or its data . Mitigation techniques are protective measures used to prevent threats or reduce their impact. This section names the common threats; later sections show how to spot them and how to reduce the damage.

scenes.title: 5.4.1 Common Security Threats (Malware, Phishing, DoS) · 2
scenes.body: Malware types in one line each: a virus attaches to files and spreads when you share them; a worm spreads by itself across a network; spyware secretly watches you; ransomware locks your files and demands money; a Trojan pretends to be useful software but hides harm. Social engineering means tricking a person , not breaking a lock with maths. Phishing is the most common exam example. Three high-yield threats: phishing (fake messages), DoS (server overload), identity theft (stolen CNIC or bank details).

scenes.title: 5.4.2 Identifying Security Threats
scenes.body: Identifying security threats means noticing signs that data or systems may be at risk. Early identification helps you act before serious damage occurs. The first line of defence is also simple behaviour: avoid unsafe downloads, cracked software, unverified websites and infected USB drives . Worked example: read the signs in a college computer lab in Khairpur. Three PCs show pop-ups and Word files have vanished after students used a “game” USB. → Treat as malware .

scenes.title: 5.4.3 Apply Mitigation Techniques
scenes.body: Mitigation techniques are actions taken to prevent security threats or reduce their harmful effects once identified. Technology helps, but it cannot stop all threats if the user is careless. Worked example: match each threat to a mitigation — BISE e-test week at a college in Larkana. Five shields: A-F, P-2, E, B, U. Antivirus+Firewall, Passwords+2FA, Encryption, Backups, User awareness. Ransomware is why backups matter: if files are locked, a clean copy brings them back.

scenes.title: 5.5 Equity and Equal Access in Digital Collaboration
scenes.body: Collaboration tools are vital for online learning and teamwork. To use these tools fairly, all users must participate without barriers . You must understand the difference between equal access and equity . Equal access Giving everyone the exact same opportunity, tools and resources. Example: providing every student with the same login ID to access a Zoom class. Equity Giving additional, specific support to users who need it, so they can reach the same outcome .
scenes.urdu: مساوی رسائی (Equal Access) سب کو ایک جیسے اوزار دیتی ہے، جیسے ایک ہی زوم لاگ ان۔ انصاف (Equity) ضرورت مند کو اضافی مدد دیتی ہے تاکہ وہی نتیجہ نکل سکے، جیسے سماعت کی مشکل والے طالب علم کے لیے زندہ ذیلی عنوانات (Captions)۔ منصفانہ تعاون کے لیے دونوں چاہییں۔

scenes.title: 5.5 Equity and Equal Access in Digital Collaboration · 3
scenes.body: Equal access: every student receives the same Zoom ID and password. That is fair in the sense of “same tool,” but a student with hearing loss still cannot follow the spoken lecture, and a student in a village with a weak 2G signal cannot join video. Equity: the teacher turns on captions, posts a low-size audio recording, and accepts the assignment as a Google Doc in the browser (not only through a heavy app). Now those two students can reach the same learning outcome . Equal = same tools.

scenes.title: 5.5.1 Functions of Equity and Equal Access
scenes.body: Equity and equal access are not slogans. They do work in a digital classroom. The source lists four functions. Worked example: design four functions for one class WhatsApp + Classroom group in Nawabshah. Need-based support: Ali is visually impaired — share materials as selectable text (not only photos) so a screen reader can speak them; add a short audio description of each diagram. Remove barriers: post a 5 MB audio summary instead of a 200 MB video for students on expensive mobile data.

scenes.title: Entrepreneurship in the Digital Age
scenes.body: Chapter 6 This chapter shows you how a real problem in your home, college or bazaar can become a business idea, and how you can test that idea cheaply with paper sketches, prototypes and a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) before you spend a lot of money. You will also learn how to choose your first users, the beachhead market, and how to collect feedback honestly and safely.

scenes.title: 6.1 Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship
scenes.body: An entrepreneur is a person who identifies a problem , thinks of a solution , and tries to change that solution into a product or service . An entrepreneur does not always begin with a large company or a big office. Many begin with a small idea, limited resources, and a strong wish to solve a problem. Think of a young person in Karachi who starts by delivering home-cooked lunch boxes to a few offices, or a student in Sukkur who repairs mobile phones for neighbours. They started small.

scenes.title: 6.1 Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship · 2
scenes.body: Entrepreneurs usually show three habits: They observe people and listen to their needs. They notice what annoys people again and again. They take calculated risks. A calculated risk is a risk you take after thinking about what you could lose and how to keep that loss small. It is not gambling. They improve their idea step by step. They do not expect the first attempt to be perfect. What is entrepreneurship? Entrepreneurship is the process of planning, starting, testing, and improving a business idea.

scenes.title: 6.2 Entrepreneurship in the Digital Age
scenes.body: Entrepreneurship in the digital age means using digital tools to start, test, improve, and grow a business idea. These tools may include mobile phones, social media, websites, online forms, digital payments, maps, videos, and simple apps . In Pakistan you already know many of them: WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Google Forms, Google Maps, and digital payments such as JazzCash, Easypaisa or Raast. The power of digital tools A digital entrepreneur does not always need to create a complex mobile app .

scenes.title: 6.3 From Problem to Business Idea
scenes.body: A good business idea usually starts from observing daily life . Look around your home, college, market, village, or city and ask these simple questions: What problem do people face? Who faces this problem? How often does it happen? What do people currently do to solve it? Can technology help in a simple way? A short way to remember them: What? Who? How often? Current fix? Tech help? Example scenario (from the source): study material before exams. Students cannot find study material before exams.

Tech help? Yes: a simple subject-wise notes organizer where all files are placed in one location (for example, one shared Google Drive folder per subject).

scenes.title: 6.4 Prototype
scenes.body: A prototype is an early model of a product, service, website, or app. It shows how the idea may look or work . It is NOT the final product . It is made to test the idea and collect feedback . Think of the clay model an architect makes before building a house, or the sample kameez a tailor stitches before making 50 for a shop. The model lets people say "make this bigger" or "move that here" before real money is spent. Why is a prototype useful?
scenes.urdu: پروٹوٹائپ (Prototype) کسی پراڈکٹ، سروس، ویب سائٹ یا ایپ کا ابتدائی نمونہ ہوتا ہے جو دکھاتا ہے کہ خیال کیسا نظر آئے گا یا کیسے کام کرے گا۔ یہ حتمی پراڈکٹ نہیں ہوتا بلکہ خیال کو آزمانے اور رائے (Feedback) لینے کے لیے بنایا جاتا ہے۔ یہ کاغذ کا خاکہ، گتے کا ماڈل، پاورپوائنٹ یا…

scenes.title: 6.4 Prototype · 2
scenes.body: A prototype helps students and entrepreneurs explain their idea clearly , because users can see something instead of only listening to words. It makes the idea visible. It helps the team find mistakes early. Users can point out if a button is hard to find, if a screen has too much text, or if a feature is missing. It saves time and money before final coding begins. Fixing a pencil sketch takes a minute; fixing finished code can take days. What form can a prototype take?

scenes.body: A prototype may be a paper sketch , a cardboard model , a clickable PowerPoint , a Canva design , a Figma wireframe , a simple website layout , or a sample service process chart . A wireframe is a simple outline drawing of a screen that shows where things go (boxes, buttons, text) without colours or pictures. For example, for a canteen pre-order system , students can just draw the screens on paper .

scenes.title: 6.5 Types of Prototypes
scenes.body: Prototypes are commonly divided into three types according to their level of detail, called fidelity . Fidelity means how close the prototype is to the final product. Low fidelity = far from final; high fidelity = very close to final. 6.5.1 Low-Fidelity Prototype A quick and rough model made at the very beginning . It is drawn on paper . It does not focus on colours or fonts . It shows the main idea and flow (which screen comes after which).
scenes.urdu: فِڈیلیٹی (Fidelity) کا مطلب ہے کہ پروٹوٹائپ حتمی پراڈکٹ سے کتنا ملتا جلتا ہے۔ لو فِڈیلیٹی کاغذ پر بنایا گیا سستا اور جلدی بننے والا خاکہ ہے؛ مڈ فِڈیلیٹی پاورپوائنٹ، کینوا یا فگما میں بنتا ہے اور اسکرینوں کے درمیان آنا جانا (Navigation) دکھاتا ہے؛ ہائی فِڈیلیٹی بالکل اصل…

scenes.title: 6.6 Prototype Development Cycle
scenes.body: Prototype development is not a one-time activity . A prototype is created, tested, improved, and tested again . This repeating process is called iteration . The main stages are Design, Build, Test, and Iterate . The prototype development cycle: Design → Build → Test → Iterate, then back to Design. Worked example: two rounds of the cycle. A team in Thatta wants a WhatsApp catalogue for a local Ajrak shop. Round 1 Design: The problem is that customers do not know which designs and prices are available.

scenes.title: 6.6 Prototype Development Cycle · 2
scenes.body: Plan: one page per design with photo, price and an "Order" message. Build: They make a paper booklet with 6 hand-drawn "catalogue pages". Test: They show it to 5 customers. Three ask, "Is this single or double-sided Ajrak? What size?" Iterate: They add size and type to every page. Round 2 Design: Add the size and type fields, and a delivery note. Build: They make the catalogue in WhatsApp Business with real photos. Test: 5 new customers browse it. Now nobody asks about size; one says the delivery charge is unclear.

scenes.title: 6.8 Minimum Viable Product (MVP)
scenes.body: A Minimum Viable Product (MVP) is the simplest working version of a product. It includes only the most important features needed to test the idea with real users . Minimum: it has only the essential features. No extras. Viable: it is usable enough to actually solve the main problem. ("Viable" means able to work successfully.) An MVP is not the final product . It is also not only a drawing . It is a small working version used to test whether users actually need the solution. Example from the source: canteen app.

scenes.title: 6.9 Difference between Prototype and MVP
scenes.body: Prototype and MVP are related, but not the same . A prototype is mainly used to show and test the design of an idea. An MVP is used to test real use and market demand . Market demand means whether enough people want the product and will use (or pay for) it. Usually a prototype comes first and an MVP comes after it: Problem → Idea → Prototype → Feedback → MVP.

scenes.title: 6.10 Identifying the Riskiest Assumption
scenes.body: Every business idea is based on assumptions . An assumption is something we believe to be true, but have not tested yet . The riskiest assumption is the belief that can make the entire business fail if it turns out to be wrong. Entrepreneurs should identify and test the riskiest assumption early , because it saves time and money . If it is wrong, you find out before building everything else.

scenes.title: 6.11 Developing an MVP
scenes.body: To develop an MVP, the team must select only the essential features . Extra features should be avoided at the beginning. A common mistake is trying to build everything at once . This makes the product difficult, costly, and slow . An MVP plan should clearly explain: the problem , target users , main feature , basic design , estimated cost , marketing method , feedback method , and improvement plan .

scenes.title: 6.13 Testing an MVP
scenes.body: MVP testing means giving the basic working version to real users and studying their response . The team should collect both numbers and comments . Numbers (quantitative data) show how many users tried the MVP and how many may use it again. Comments (qualitative data) explain what users liked, disliked, or found confusing. Testing should be planned before the MVP is launched . Decide: How many users will test it. How long the test will continue. What information will be collected.

scenes.title: 6.14 Beachhead Market
scenes.body: A beachhead market is a small and focused group of first users . These users have a clear need and are likely to try the product early . Instead of trying to serve everyone, entrepreneurs first focus on one small group . This helps them test the MVP properly and improve it before expanding . The word comes from the army: a beachhead is the small piece of beach soldiers capture first when they land; from there they move inland. In business, your beachhead is the first small group you "win".

scenes.title: 6.14 Beachhead Market · 2
scenes.body: Characteristics of a good beachhead market It should be specific and narrowly defined . It should be reachable by the startup team. The users should have a strong, immediate need for the solution. For example, targeting " all students in Pakistan " is too broad for a new study app. " Grade XII students preparing for board exams in one college " is much more focused and easier to reach. Start with the small inner circle (beachhead), learn and improve, then expand outward.

scenes.title: 6.15 Complete Student Project
scenes.body: You will work in groups and complete one small entrepreneurship project. The project should be simple, local, and possible in the classroom . The purpose is to practise the complete journey : problem → prototype → feedback → MVP plan → risky assumption → beachhead market. Suggested project ideas: homework and test reminder system, college notice organizer, canteen pre-order system, small shop WhatsApp catalogue, college van update system, lost and found item reporting system, study notes organizer.

scenes.title: 6.15 Complete Student Project · 3
scenes.body: Mistake: Writing an MVP plan that lists every feature of the dream app. The rubric marks this as "Confused with the final product". Fix: Keep the MVP to the essential feature(s) and add a clear testing plan (how many users, how long, what you will measure). 1. Name four suggested project ideas. 2. What does "Excellent" look like for Problem ID in the rubric? 3. Which rubric level says "Confused with the final product"? Answers: 1.

scenes.title: 6.16 Ethical and Safe Use of Digital Tools
scenes.body: Digital entrepreneurship should be responsible . When collecting user feedback, you must respect: Privacy : people's personal information belongs to them. Truthfulness : report results honestly; do not make up numbers or hide bad feedback. Fairness : treat all users equally. You should not collect unnecessary personal information or share phone numbers or photos without permission . Equity point A good digital solution should consider users who have weak internet , limited devices , or language difficulty .
scenes.urdu: ڈیجیٹل کاروبار ذمہ داری سے کرنا چاہیے۔ رائے جمع کرتے وقت لوگوں کی رازداری (Privacy)، سچائی اور انصاف کا خیال رکھیں؛ غیر ضروری ذاتی معلومات نہ لیں اور اجازت کے بغیر فون نمبر یا تصاویر شیئر نہ کریں۔ اچھا حل کمزور انٹرنیٹ، محدود موبائل اور زبان کی مشکل والے لوگوں کا بھی خیال…
scenes.speak: Digital entrepreneurship should be responsible . When collecting user feedback, you must respect: Privacy : people's personal information belongs to them. Truthfulness : report results honestly; do not make up numbers or hide bad feedback. Fairness : treat all users equally. You should not collect unnecessary personal information or share phone numbers or photos without permission . Equity point A good digital solution should consider users who have weak internet , limited devices , or language difficulty .

scenes.title: 6.16 Ethical and Safe Use of Digital Tools · 2
scenes.body: A design with large buttons , simple Urdu/Sindhi instructions , and low data usage helps ensure equal access . Equity means making sure everyone, including people with fewer resources, can use the solution. Worked example: fix an unethical feedback form. A team's canteen feedback form asks: Full name, father's name, CNIC/B-form number, home address. → Problem: unnecessary personal data. Fix: ask only class (or nothing personal at all). "Upload your selfie." → Problem: photos are not needed and could be misused.

scenes.title: 6.16 Ethical and Safe Use of Digital Tools · 3
scenes.body: Fix: remove. The team plans to post all respondents' phone numbers in the class group. → Problem: sharing numbers without permission. Fix: never share; keep responses private to the team. The form is in English only and has a 5 MB video at the top. → Problem: excludes users with language difficulty or weak internet. Fix: add Urdu/Sindhi instructions and remove the heavy video. When presenting, the team reports "30 out of 40 would use it again" exactly, without rounding it up to "almost everyone".

scenes.title: Career Opportunities
scenes.body: This unit covered entrepreneurship in the digital age, turning problems into business ideas, prototyping, building MVPs, and identifying beachhead markets. Mastery of these concepts opens the door to careers in startups and digital innovation . Pakistan has many incubators (for example, National Incubation Centres, NICs, in major cities) that support young founders. Worked example: match the task to the career.
scenes.urdu: اس باب کی مہارتیں اسٹارٹ اپ اور ڈیجیٹل جدت کے شعبوں میں روزگار کے دروازے کھولتی ہیں، جیسے اسٹارٹ اپ بانی، پراڈکٹ مینیجر، بزنس اینالسٹ، اسٹارٹ اپ کنسلٹنٹ، ڈیجیٹل مارکیٹنگ ماہر اور انکیوبیٹر اینالسٹ۔ ان سب کاموں میں صارف کو سمجھنا، مفروضے آزمانا اور چھوٹے پیمانے سے شروع کرنا…

scenes.title: Career Opportunities · 2
scenes.body: "Decide whether the canteen app should add payments next or a weekly menu." → Product Manager (prioritising features). "Run a WhatsApp and Instagram campaign to get the first 100 users in one college." → Digital Marketing Specialist . "Review 20 student startup pitches and pick 5 for incubation." → Venture / Incubator Analyst . Every career in the table uses the same chapter skills: understand users, test assumptions, start small . Mistake: Thinking startup careers are only for programmers.
